text:
Meta Just Paid Nearly $17 Billion To Make Sure It Gets To Write The Kid Safety Rules For Every Other Social Media Platform | Mike Masnick, Techdirt

By now you’ve almost certainly heard the news that Meta has settled with 52 state and local Attorneys General who had sued the company in some form or another over child safety on Meta’s platforms. The headlines are all covering the basics: the years-long case these states filed against Meta ends, and Meta pays somewhere between $12.7 billion and $18 billion, depending on which document you read (the consent judgment itself caps the total at $16,680,647,753.21; Meta’s press release rounds it up to “approximately $18 billion”). Also Meta will implement a bunch of changes to its platforms with the aim of improving child safety on those platforms. It will also “encourage” YouTube and TikTok to enable the same safety features even though (bizarrely), if YouTube and TikTok follow suit, then Meta will have to pay more.

You can read the details of the proposed settlement here.

https://t.co/VyWIPJ3Yxz

Notably, the whole point of doing this as a “settlement” is that everyone involved knows full well that no government could mandate these feature changes without violating the First Amendment. But now that it’s in a “settlement” the courts may need to explore if these choices — which Meta could make freely on its own — suddenly have become a “state action,” implicating the First Amendment.

As with the various rulings against Meta over the last few months, people are cheering this on, without realizing the damage it will do. We’ll explore why this is problematic in a moment, but just to highlight that I’m not alone in thinking so, both EFF and Fight for the Future are warning how bad this settlement is. Here’s EFF:

Under this settlement, young users will now have less access to Meta products, and a lesser ability to exercise their rights to speak, access information and art and culture, associate and form communities, and play. The settlement also embeds age assurance into every product, mandating the collection of even more personal information from users of all ages; this enshrines Meta’s harmful surveillance into law, and it will compromise users’ privacy and anonymity while increasing their exposure to data breaches and government data requests. And the data minimization and security measures don’t keep states from using data collected under the agreement for other law enforcement purposes – which could include things like criminal investigations of abortions or gender-affirming care.

And here’s Fight’s emailed statement:

Big Tech does pose harm to our kids through its business practices and exploitation, but pushing for more censorship, age-gating, and surveillance of young people at the hands of the same Big Tech companies that have already harmed young people is not the answer. Online ID checks when implemented put vital information behind age-gates, stamp down teenagers’ right to speak, and expose all of us to even more of our data being collected, hacked, and leaked. Meta knows that managing this amount of personal information and enforcing these agegates will be messy and that’s why they are seeking to offload the burden to anyone but themselves, while being seen to comply by the public and lawmakers. Instead of actually damaging their exploitative business model, this result allows Meta to bring everyone else down with them, from app stores to other social media companies. We feared that these lawsuits would manufacture consent for invasive age verification and content controls and our fears have been proven correct. We will continue to oppose online ID checks everywhere and be on the watch for more censorship creeping into Meta’s platform.

We’ll get into the specifics of why this settlement is so bad, but first some important background. For a few decades now, when basically all Attorneys General would get together to threaten and/or sue tech companies, it was almost always over bullshit headline grabbing claims where the AGs either had no jurisdiction or ability to legally do anything. Sixteen years ago, we wrote one story about an account written by a CEO of a company who faced down dozens of state AGs who were way more concerned about the headlines they generated than actually making platforms safe.

It was similar to other stories that we’d heard, where no matter what companies did to explain to the AGs what steps they were taking to keep a platform safe the AGs would simply turn around and misrepresent what they were told, out of context, to make the platforms look worse and worse until they agreed to some sort of settlement. It happened with Craigslist. It happened with ISPs being forced to kick their users off at the behest of the recording industry. Even John Oliver has covered how grandstanding state Attorneys General will target just about anyone they want to shake down in some form or another.

That’s not to say that there aren’t righteous cases brought by Attorneys General, but there are so many examples of them being much more about getting headlines than actually making people safer. And the simple fact is that these efforts are so resource intensive, so expensive, and so draining that it’s no surprise that most companies end up “settling” by agreeing to do things that the government simply cannot force a company to do. But because it’s a “settlement” people act like it’s not the government doing it.

In this case, given some of the recent court decisions, it’s no surprise that Meta would strike some sort of settlement. As these cases continued, the headlines would only get worse for the company. And Meta deserves some bad headlines, but as I’ve discussed, many of the bad headlines in these cases involved lawyers and the media taking things way out of context. The classic case with Meta is that many of its efforts to study how to make its platforms safer were used against the company as proof that “they knew!” their platforms were unsafe!

The lesson for the rest of the tech industry is grim and unambiguous: never study whether your own platform is causing harm. The mere existence of the research will be turned into Exhibit A that “they knew,” both in the court of public opinion and in actual courts.

The other bit of background worth understanding here is that Meta has been desperately seeking a path to regulatory capture for quite some time now. It’s been practically begging for Congress to pass child safety legislation that only the largest companies (like itself) could comply with. Indeed, Meta has done this before. It went against the rest of the internet industry in embracing FOSTA, again to try to create a regulatory moat. So this shouldn’t be surprising.

Meta’s failed forays into the “metaverse” and AI have shown that it’s been pretty consistently losing the innovation race, and the government granting it a regulatory moat that smaller competitors can’t cross would be a godsend.

And it’s even better when it can be done in a way that looks like Meta “losing” a lawsuit.

So that’s what Meta gets here. They “settle” the lawsuit so the AGs and Meta haters can all claim that they’ve “protected the children.” Meta pays out over a decade — enough that it’s taking a $10 billion legal charge in Q3, which stings for a bit but will mostly be forgotten by next year. Meta can easily eat the cost. And then Meta agrees to implement a bunch of kid safety features, most of which we have no idea whether they actually protect any kids. Notably, a legislature could not have mandated most of these features without running straight into the First Amendment — but coming out of a settlement, they carry the imprimatur of law anyway (more on that in a moment), and the structure of the agreement makes it so that Meta has to actively encourage Google and TikTok to take identical steps, thereby setting in concrete what steps any platform will have to take to be considered following “best practices” and therefore acceptable to most of the country’s Attorneys General.

The specific features don’t even matter that much, but for the record:

- Time Limit: A default two-hour daily time limit that teens can only turn off with a parent’s permission. This limit is cumulative across Facebook and Instagram, and time spent scrolling on both apps counts toward the total, including if we detect that someone has multiple accounts.

- Night Mode: A default block from our apps between midnight and 6am. This means teens will not be able to post or view their Feed, Stories, Explore, or Reels, for example.

- School Mode: Notifications will be muted by default between 8 AM and 3 PM. During those hours, teens will no longer receive push notifications, except for direct messages and alerts about their account security or safety.

- Regular Prompts: Teens will receive prompts after every 15 minutes of continuous screen time on Facebook or Instagram. They’ll also receive prompts when their total daily usage hits 60 minutes and 90 minutes. These prompts are designed to encourage intentional use.

- Algorithmic Feed Control: Teens will be able to choose a non-algorithmic feed — one that isn’t personalized by our recommendation systems — as their default. We will periodically remind them of this option, and parents can choose to adjust their teen’s default experience to require this setting.

- Autoplay Control: Teens will be able to turn off autoplay, so that content no longer automatically plays. Instead, they’ll need to take a deliberate action, like a tap or swipe, to see more. Parents can choose to adjust their teen’s default experience to require this setting.

- Hidden Likes: Teens won’t see the number of likes and reactions on posts — both their own and those from others — by default.

- Disabling cosmetic surgery and extreme makeup filters: In addition to our existing policy to block teens from using cosmetic surgery filters, we’ll now block teens from using extreme makeup filters.

- Age Assurance: We work hard to find and remove underage accounts from our apps and, as part of our agreement, we’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to under-13s. We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may be between the ages of 13 and 17, so we can ensure those accounts are placed in experiences designed for teens, even if they give us an adult birthday. However, to ensure teens are consistently protected across the many apps they use, app stores must provide developers with verified age information. This will allow platforms to put age-appropriate protections in place for as many teens as possible. That’s why we’ll continue to advocate for legislation that empowers parents by requiring app stores to verify age and obtain parental approval before a teen downloads an app.

- Age-appropriate content restrictions: We will maintain our current content standards so that, by default, teens are placed into 13+ content settings, inspired by movie ratings criteria and parent feedback. We will also continue to prevent teens from following or interacting with accounts we consider age-inappropriate. We will work to continually improve these systems to ensure age-appropriate content experiences for teens.

- Unwanted contact from strangers: We will maintain our current practices of defaulting teens into private accounts on Instagram and private default settings on Facebook, and we’ll continue to restrict potentially suspicious adults from contacting them. We will also strengthen our efforts to make it harder for those adults to find, follow, or interact with teens.

- Reporting and ongoing protection from harmful content: We will continue to give teens easy ways to report content that concerns them, and we’ll work to improve our response times. We will also continue our work to protect teens from potentially harmful experiences by regularly evaluating how often teens are exposed to them. We’ll draw on research and expert input to improve our work.

- Strengthening our parental controls: We will encourage parents to set up our supervision tools and give them new controls and insights. This includes notifying parents when a teen links a secondary account, alerting them to interactions with potentially suspicious accounts, and providing periodic updates on their teen’s usage and any changes their teen attempts to make to their protective settings.

Some of those might be good features. Some of them might not be. Some of them might be good for some kids, but very bad for other kids.

Part of the problem is we really don’t know.

There is something of an accountability structure here too. Meta and the states will appoint an “independent” auditor for five years, and the age assurance system gets tested annually to meet certain thresholds. But it’s important to look at what’s actually being audited here. It’s whether or not Meta is implementing the things it’s promised to do, not whether any of those things actually work.

But now these are, effectively, mandated by law. Even though if Congress or the states had passed a law requiring these, it would almost certainly be thrown out as unconstitutional under the First Amendment.

The weirdest part of the agreement is that Meta has to try to convince Google (YouTube) and TikTok to implement some (but not all?) of these same features. Indeed, Meta has already put up a settlement-mandated open letter to those two companies asking them to implement those features.

What’s so weird is that if YouTube and TikTok agree to do this and to voluntarily throw billions of dollars at the states, then Meta also needs to pay more. The breakdown of the money Meta owes is partially dependent on them arm-twisting those two companies to do the same things:

The agreement includes a payment of approximately $18 billion, which can be used to fund youth online safety initiatives, among other state priorities. The payment will be distributed in annual installments over a 10-year period. Participating states will receive approximately 70% (approximately $12.7 billion) of the allocated payment over the decade. The remaining 30% (approximately $5.3 billion) will be released only after two specific conditions are met.

1. YouTube and TikTok implement a one-hour Daily Limit, Night Mode, and age assurance measures.

2. YouTube and TikTok each pay an amount matching the 30% figure, with half of the remaining funds tied to YouTube’s payment and half tied to TikTok’s.

You can argue that Meta might not actually want YouTube and TikTok to do this, so they won’t have to pay that extra $5.3 billion, but from a competitive standpoint, you have to think that Meta absolutely needs to have YouTube and TikTok implement these features or its already somewhat dwindling market share will dwindle faster.

It’s quite possible that YouTube and TikTok will go along with this, rather than get bogged down in a similarly costly legal fight. But, again, that would create many problems. First, we still don’t know if those feature changes are actually helpful or effective. But now they’re effectively government mandated.

In theory, this could open up room for other platforms to come in and sweep up the youth market by not implementing these same features. But the nature of this agreement is that if the state AGs suddenly feel like any platform is becoming too popular with the kids, it can point to this agreement and call it “industry standard” or “industry best practices” to insinuate that other companies not doing the same are deliberately choosing to keep kids unsafe.

Indeed, within the agreement there’s a bit of weirdness, in which Meta has to push for “industry wide adoption” which is currently defined as YouTube and TikTok, but which the agreement makes clear could include any new social media platform if such a new platform meets the thresholds. In other words, Meta is basically being forced into guaranteeing this settlement creates an industry-wide standard.

And that’s a real problem when we still don’t know how to actually help keep kids safer online. So if a web service comes up with a unique or innovative or different idea that works differently than what Meta has agreed to do, then that may be too risky to even try. Better to just follow what the AGs have “blessed” in this settlement.

As noted, we already know that some of these things are directly harmful. Age assurance is a privacy nightmare. Enshrining it as the industry standard means the end of meaningful online anonymity, and it “forces” Meta to collect more data about all of us — including adults — while handing the states a pipeline to that data for whatever else they decide it’s useful for.

That’s bad.

Also, there are some oddly specific requirements:

Meta SMPs will disable Teen Users from applying Cosmetic Procedure Filters to their content.

The agreement clarifies that this means:

… any digital filter or augmented reality (AR) effect that distorts, sculpts, redefines, or idealizes a user’s face in a way that cannot be achieved without cosmetic surgery or extreme makeup techniques.

And, sure, I can understand why such content might be unhealthy for teens. But it is, in fact, Constitutionally-protected speech. Meta could decide internally to block that speech specifically on its own platform (that’s its own editorial right). But now that it’s being done at the behest of government pressure, it almost certainly violates the First Amendment.

Also, somewhat oddly, some of the rules appear to only apply to content in English or Spanish:

With respect to Potentially Harmful Reported Content submitted in English or Spanish, Meta SMPs shall maintain processes designed to permit Teen Users to receive a response indicating Meta’s decision on the report within 6 hours in at least 90% of cases.

The implication is obvious: those are the languages most reports come in, and Meta is expected to staff up enough to clear them fast. But it also means the government has just negotiated a moderation service level that varies by the language you happen to speak — English and Spanish speakers get a six-hour guarantee, Tagalog and Mandarin speakers get whatever Meta feels like. That’s a strange thing for a state to be dictating at all.

This is also a perfect example of the kind of standard that only a giant can meet. A six-hour turnaround on 90% of reports is achievable when you have thousands of trust & safety staff and a decade of tooling. For a startup with four employees and a Discord server, it’s a fantasy — and now it’s the benchmark against which every AG will measure them.

So what happens now? The judge will need to review the settlement, but I’m actually wondering if some teenage users would have standing to challenge this. Meta is clearly restricting First Amendment protected speech under this agreement. It is free to do so on its own if it chooses to do so, but this is different. Here it’s doing so because it’s being forced to by various state AGs, making it a state action.

Under the Supreme Court’s recent (unanimous) Vullo decision, that seems pretty clearly unconstitutional. In that case,the justices said, quite clearly:

[A] government official cannot do indirectly what she is barred from doing directly: A government official cannot coerce a private party to punish or suppress disfavored speech on her behalf.

That seems like it should be the whole ballgame, because that’s what’s happening here.

One other point on all of this. Here’s the list of 52 Attorneys General that have agreed to this settlement:

Alabama, Alaska, American Samoa, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, N. Mariana Islands, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.

Notice anyone missing? Yup. There’s no New Mexico. Remember, New Mexico won its initial case against Meta recently, enabling the judge to force a different set of feature changes on the company. So… now Meta may have certain features for New Mexico, and different features for everywhere else?

None of this is to say that Meta shouldn’t do a better job trying to protect kids on its platform. Obviously, it can certainly do more. But this settlement seems much more like Meta using this case as a way to force the industry into a set of required steps (which might not help much, and may do real harm in some cases), making it difficult for smaller competitors to enter the market, and giving them a bit of regulatory capture through mass lawsuit settlement.

As law professor Jess Miers wrote, this settlement is about Meta selling out the entire social media industry, forcing them to embrace impractical and unhelpful features that serve only to lock in giants and lock out upstarts:

But for all the people “celebrating” this as a win “against” Meta, you’ve been fooled. Meta just cut a deal to put itself in charge of how social media works going forward. As Justin Maurer wrote on Bluesky, this is Meta taking a “please regulate me Daddy” approach to the government, and getting exactly what it really has been asking for.

We still don’t have any actual evidence that this will help anyone, let alone every kid. The state AGs didn’t have to prove how this would help kids. Meta didn’t have to prove it. The judge won’t be asked to. It’s just taken on faith. Meta offered this up, the AGs okayed it… and it all becomes a grand experiment on kids.

You can argue that these feature changes sound like they should help kids. Limiting access to two hours a day (unless parents grant more, which many will), lights out at midnight, disappearing like counts — these all sound like they’ll help some kids. But if it turns out that locking kids out of these systems actually pushes the most vulnerable ones to darker places with no trust & safety team at all, you won’t hear about that from Meta or the AGs.

We just spent three years teaching the entire industry that if you do research on child safety, you’ll have it held against you. Do we really think that all of this is going to actually enable anyone to figure out what works to help actual kids?

Meta bought itself a moat. The AGs bought themselves headlines that will be useful next election season. And every teenager in the country was just automatically enrolled in an untested experiment. There’s a five year independent auditor requirement to confirm that Meta follows the rules. But not to see if the rules work.

Listen closely and the anthems of rock become a soundtrack of cosmic quarantine.

Elton John’s Rocket Man:

The narrator flies alone into the void, but the destination is clinical and hopeless.

🎵Mars ain’t the kind of place to raise your kids. In fact it’s cold as hell. And there’s no one there to raise them if you did🎵

🎵And all the science, I don’t understand, it’s just my job five days a week🎵

🎵a rocket man…🎵

The song is about the futility of trying to leave a sealed system.

Don Maclean’s American Pie:

🎵a generation lost in space, with no time left to start again🎵

That line is diagnosis, not metaphor.

The music dies the day the last connection to something higher is severed.

🎵no angel born in Hell could break that Satan’s spell🎵

The spell of the Stargate?

🎵Now for 10 years we’ve been on our own, and moss grows fat on a rolling stone, but that’s not how it used to be🎵

10,000 yrs maybe? Moss growing on a rolling stone, not how it used to be.?

🎵The father, Son, and the holy ghost, they caught the last train for the coast, the day the music died🎵

Abandoning the planet to its confinement.

The levee is dry.

The day the music died is the day the barrier closed and the children of the Nephilim realised their ancestral technology was shattered, leaving them to steer history from inside the cage for 10k + years.

🎵and we sang dirges in the dark🎵

The dirges are the collective memory of a people who once travelled the stars and are now permanently grounded.

The doors:

🎵you know the day destroys the night, night decides the day. Tried to run, tried to hide. Break in through to the other side🎵

Queens Bohemian Rhapsody:

🎵caught in a landslide, no escape from reality🎵

🎵open your eyes, look up to the skies and see, I’m just a poor boy🎵

The poor boy looks up to the skies and sees only the sealed dome.

🎵mama just killed a man, put a gun against his head, pulled the trigger now he’s dead. Mama life had just begun. But now I’ve gone and thrown it all away🎵

🎵too late, my time has come, sends shivers down my spine, body’s aching all the time, goodbye to everybody, I’ve got to go, gotta leave you all behind and face the truth🎵

Then when he begs to leave, the answer is absolute:

🎵Bismillah! We will not let you go… Never let me go? Beelzebub has a devil put aside for me..🎵

The force that erected the barrier will not open it.

🎵just gotta get out, just gotta get right outta here🎵

Fleetwood Mac’s “Landslide” asks the question:

🎵oh mirror in the sky, what is love? Can the child within my heart rise above🎵

The sky itself is the mirror, the reflective surface of the etheric shield.

The children of the Nephilim looks upwards and wonders whether any part of the original nature can still transcend the quarantine.

The barrier answers with silence.

Linkin Park’s album covers offer some clues.

“Hybrid theory” and “Meteora”

The Eagles Hotel California:

🎵the shimmering light ahead could be heaven or it could be hell🎵

Exactly the ambiguity of the Stargate that looks like a doorway but is a cage.

🎵you can check-out any time you like, but you can never leave🎵

These songs, and hundreds more, are not coincidences.

They are coded transmissions from inside the cage.

text:
The Stargate Quarantine:

When the pursuers of the Nephilim shattered Tiamat, they fled our solar system to escape the cosmic chaos they had unleashed. Yet for reasons of their own they took extraordinary precautions to ensure that any enemies who might still live on our planet could never leave.

They sealed Earth behind a powerful etheric barrier, an impenetrable shield that still stands.

No one on this planet can physically breach it.

The Nephilim arrived roughly 50,000 years ago, refugees from systems that may have included Draco or Alpha Draconis. The cataclysmic pole shift and the war of the gods followed about 13,500 years ago. They did not come by choice. Their hunters, racing to escape the planetary upheaval, erected the membrane as a final quarantine: if any Nephilim remained, they would never again spread their corruption across the galaxy.

That barrier is the true Stargate.

Not a doorway out, but a cage.

Ancient texts describe it. In the Pistis Sophia, the outer darkness appears as a vast Dragon with its tail in its mouth, the uroboros, the encircling serpent that guards the globe like a pearl. Native American lore calls it the great web in the sky. Even the United Nations seal represents the image: Earth locked inside a strange grid and framed by laurel leaves.

Revelation 8 records: “And the fifth angel sounded, and I saw a star fall from heaven unto the earth: and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit.”

2 Peter states that God cast the sinning angels into hell and chained them in darkness until judgment.

Earth is that pit.

Those carrying Nephilim DNA cannot leave. They remain contained until the appointed time.

The assassinated researcher Bill Cooper wrote that no man has ever ascended higher than roughly 300 miles in any publicly known program. No man has orbited, landed on, or walked the Moon under NASA’s claimed technology. Radiation belts, cosmic rays, vacuum, and surface temperatures exceeding 265 °C in full sunlight make it impossible with our present science. The Apollo landings were theater. If anyone has reached the Moon, it was done in secret and by far different means.

The Stargate is tied to the Moon’s orbit. Research indicates that around 30,000 years ago a highly developed civilisation thrived in the Andes, and the Moon was not yet present. This supports the case that our satellite is no natural body but an artificial construction parked in place thousands of years ago.

The idea is less far-fetched than it first appears. Across the solar system the moons of Saturn, Uranus and the rest are tiny escorts. Ours is vastly larger, closer in scale to a small planetoid than to any ordinary satellite.

Nostradamus, the French clairvoyant, wrote: “He will come to take himself to the corner of Luna where he will be taken and placed on alien land.”

Even the Lunar Society, founded by Erasmus Darwin (father of Charles Darwin), met only at the full moon.

By the Renaissance the alien progeny finally understood the barrier. Their ancestral technology had been shattered. For eleven thousand years they had steered history, raised empires, enslaved populations, and forced technological progress while keeping humanity sexually, genetically, and psychologically stunted. They rebuilt the hardware only to discover that the cage was still locked.

What technology erected, they believed technology could dismantle. The major dynasties of the planet funded occultists, scientists, and philosophers to crack the Stargate. The perfect cover was science itself, and occultism itself. Most practitioners today still do not know whom their work truly serves. Fronts, legends, and double lives conceal the real project, just as every major criminal syndicate operates.

The barrier remains.

The quarantine holds.

The children of the Nephilim are still here, still digging, still waiting for a way out that may never come.

text:
The United States has just surpassed its highest annual measles case count in more than thirty years, making this a critical moment for public health monitoring. From a biological perspective, this outbreak offers a stark, real-time lesson in population dynamics and viral transmission.

Measles is considered one of the most contagious human pathogens on the planet. When an infected person breathes or coughs, the virus can remain suspended and active in the air for up to two hours. If unprotected individuals enter that airspace, the pathogen will successfully infect roughly ninety percent of them. Because the virus is so aggressively efficient, a community requires a strict ninety-five percent immunity rate to effectively block its spread and protect vulnerable individuals.

The current data perfectly illustrates what happens when that defensive wall cracks. With localized immunization rates dipping below that critical threshold, the virus is rapidly exploiting those gaps, predominantly infecting unvaccinated children and young adults. This historic resurgence is a clear reminder that when it comes to highly evolved airborne viruses, mathematics and biology always dictate the outcome.

Reference: Jacobson KB, Goddard K, Bartlett J, et al. Geographic Variation in Measles Vaccine Coverage Among Children Aged 7 Years in Northern California. JAMA Netw Open. 2026;9(7):e2626224. DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.26224

text:
Heard of a California real estate “we buy houses” investor who made a mint using this kind of “direct” strategy.

The way that game usually works:

You send thousands of mailers to prospective home sellers.

The mail piece would usually say something like, “if you’re interested in selling your house — give me a call at xyz.”

Then the prospects would call in and the investor would start screening them over the phone, asking a million and one questions about their situations and their house.

This guy decided to change the game…

Simply by sending cold prospects a real legitimate offer in the mail — the exact price he’d pay, cash, in seven days — or whatever the offer.

No long-ass phone screening. No warm up message.

Just the offer.

People would call in and say, “don’t you want to see my house first?” or… “is this offer real?”

Dude was a pro who knew the market like the back of his hand, plus he was moving 10-plus houses a month.

So he knew he’d overpay for some, underpay for others, but as long as he was making a ton of good offers every day — business was booming.

No need for all the “throat-clearing” copy that everyone else was doing.

Lesson.

text:
$AAPL down 8% on supply chain issues and memory shortages $MU

Apple Inc. tumbled in late trading after component shortages weighed on the company’s sales forecast, signaling that industrywide supply constraints are taking a bigger toll than anticipated.

Revenue will rise 9% to 11% in the fiscal fourth quarter, which is lower than analysts' estimates of more than 12% growth, due to constraints affecting Macs, iPhones, and iPads.

The disappointing forecast sent Apple shares down about 7% in premarket trading on Friday, despite total sales topping estimates and climbing 16% to $109.4 billion.

Apple has been struggling to secure enough computer processors and counter fast-rising memory costs, a situation that forced the company to raise prices on Macs and iPads last month.

The supply crunch has also led to extended wait times on key computers like the Mac mini and Mac Studio. On the call, Chief Executive Officer Tim Cook said constraints would affect more Macs, iPhones and iPads in the current quarter. Currency fluctuations are hampering growth as well.

The disappointing forecast sent Apple shares down about 7% in premarket trading on Friday.

Cook likened the memory cost issue to a “100-year flood,” while adding that the chip shortages were fueled by higher-than-expected demand for the iPhone and Mac. He specifically cited consumer interest in the iPhone 17 line and MacBook Neo, a new low-cost laptop.

Apple also said services growth would decelerate in the September quarter. And it warned of an impact from regulatory changes to its App Store business model in the European Union and elsewhere. New legislation allows developers to collect subscription payments directly, bypassing Apple’s fee. Gaming revenue was softer than anticipated, too.

In addition, the tech giant’s results showed weaker-than-expected revenue in China and from services during the June quarter. China sales amounted to $18.8 billion, short of the $19.6 billion estimated by some analysts.

Revenue from services grew a disappointing 12% to $30.7 billion, compared with a $31.4 billion projection. That business includes Apple Music, the App Store, iCloud subscriptions, streaming video and other digital offerings.

Still, total sales topped estimates, climbing 16% to $109.4 billion.

The quarter serves as a swan song of sorts for Cook, who will hand the reins to hardware head John Ternus on Sept. 1. Cook, Apple’s leader since 2011, diversified the product lineup and increased annual sales to nearly half a trillion dollars.

The quarter serves as a swan song of sorts for Cook, who will hand the reins to hardware head John Ternus on Sept. 1. Cook, Apple’s leader since 2011, diversified the product lineup and increased annual sales to nearly half a trillion dollars.

The iPhone, Apple’s biggest moneymaker, was a bright spot last quarter. The product’s revenue rose 22% to $54.3 billion during the period, topping estimates of $53.6 billion. The numbers suggest that demand remains solid for the iPhone 17 series launched last September. The company also rolled out a new low-end 17e model in March.

Earnings rose to $2.02 a share in the third quarter, which ended June 27. That compared with an average projection of $1.89 a share.

Mac revenue came in at about $10.4 billion, growing 29% from a year earlier. That marks another highlight and is an area of particular importance to Ternus. The company launched new Macs in March, including the MacBook Neo, M5 versions of the MacBook Pro and a fresh MacBook Air. Wall Street was looking for $8.62 billion.

The iPad brought in sales of $6.19 billion, missing estimates of $6.89 billion. Apple launched a new iPad Air in March and an updated iPad Pro last October. But both those upgrades were built around new chips, rather than major design changes.

Apple is planning several new Macs and iPads across the end of this year and next spring that could help boost sales. They include the first touch-screen MacBook and a revamped iPad mini, part of end-to-end refreshes to both product lines.

Apple’s wearables, home and accessories category brought in revenue of $7.88 billion, up 6.5% from a year earlier. That matched estimates of $7.87 billion. Apple is looking to give this segment a boost in the coming months with new watches and a revamped slate of home devices, including a home hub and new TV set-top box.

The company is also making some changes to how it offers products. On Tuesday, it rolled out a device leasing program called Apple Upgrade, allowing users to essentially subscribe to iPhones, iPads and Macs and trade them in at the end of their lease terms. The program, which resembles car leasing, will likely mitigate the recent price increases for many buyers.

Ternus, a 25-year veteran of Apple, is set to take charge about two-thirds of the way through the current period. The fourth quarter is a critical one for the company because it’s when new iPhones and other major devices typically go on sale.

Ternus faces the challenge of adapting Apple to the AI era. The Cupertino, California-based company has struggled to catch up in this area, with its artificial intelligence services lagging behind those of Silicon Valley peers.

“There is so much opportunity for us, with everything that’s happening in this space, and we’re just really focused on our plans and very excited about it,” Ternus said during the call. Cook said Ternus would lead earnings calls moving forward.

The incoming CEO will have a host of new products to show off after he takes over. Apple is preparing to introduce its first foldable iPhone, smart glasses and other wearable devices.

Other challenges loom. Ternus will need to replenish Apple’s leadership bench as many of its senior executives near retirement. He’ll also have to reverse a talent drain at the company, which has lost staff to OpenAI and other AI rivals.

"Remember, the plate is a pitcher’s target and he has to come to it.
I use ‘back of plate’ expression to mean towards the catcher, away from the plate to denote distance from plate towards outside of box.
Now use a slightly closed stance and keep a little more weight on the front foot and back.
It gives you balance and won’t pull you away from corners.
You’re always going to give the maximum drive.
Do not pull a curve-ball from a right-hander.
The ball is revolving away from you.
Hit off the revolution and to right field.
If high inside fastballs really bother you:
Crouch from your waist and let them pass. Do not bite, in other words.
Squat, make the pitcher throw lower, which set it apart from the position that bothers him.
But I think with the instructions I give, you will hit the pitches wherever they land."
Ty Cobb’s advice from a letter written to Sam Chapman, a right-handed hitter, in May 1938.
"Just before I graduated from the University of California in the spring of 1938, I had three offers to play baseball.
The New York Yankees and Cincinnati Reds each offered me a $9,000 bonus;
The Philadelphia A’s offered me $6,000.
All three offered the minimum $2,500 salary for the season.
Then I got this letter from Ty Cobb, whom I’d never met.
Cobb said the best thing for me to do was to sign with Connie Mack, owner/manager of the A’s.
Cobb said he’d played 24 years in the big leagues and learned more about the game in the last two years with Mr. Mack, than in all the other years he played.
I followed his advice."
Sam Chapman.
Serving as a flyer in World War II cost Chapman four prime years, as it did many players.

text:
In July 2026, a sitting member of Congress was asked on the record to say that the October 7 attack on Israel was justified.

Rep. Ro Khanna declined. He invoked Gandhi and King.

The outlet was Drop Site News. Founded by veteran investigative journalists Ryan Grim, Jeremy Scahill, and Nausicaa Renner. Co- founder, Jeremy Scahill, accused Khanna of a double standard.

Drop Site launched in July 2024. Its first publication was an 8,000-word interview with two senior officials of Hamas — conducted nine months after Hamas murdered roughly 1,200 people in Israel, raped and mutilated women, burned families alive in their homes, and took 251 hostages.

Scahill began his career at Democracy Now!, which by its own count airs on more than 1,500 stations. He holds a Type Media Center fellowship.

Three weeks after the Khanna interview, three events take place in eight days.

August 5. The Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft hosts "Rehabilitating a Cratering Image: Israeli Influence in America."
August 11. Atria/One Signal, an imprint of Simon & Schuster, publishes Israel's Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power, by Eli Clifton and Ian S. Lustick, Bess W. Heyman Chair Emeritus in Political Science at the University of Pennsylvania.
August 12. The Nation hosts an online launch, with editor and publisher Katrina vanden Heuvel, national affairs correspondent Jeet Heer, US/Middle East Project president Daniel Levy, and both authors.

The participants' own published biographies make the architecture legible without inference.

Eli Clifton appears at all three. In Quincy's own words: "cofounder and senior advisor at the Quincy Institute... coauthor of the Center for American Progress report 'Fear Inc.: The Roots of the Islamophobia Network in America.' Clifton has been a fellow at The Nation Institute and Type Media Center."
He cofounded the institution hosting the first event.
He has held a fellowship at the institute affiliated with the magazine hosting the third.
He has held the same Type Media Center fellowship as Scahill.
Nick Cleveland-Stout moderates on August 5. In Quincy's own words: "a research associate in the Democratizing Foreign Policy program at the Quincy Institute... He investigates foreign influence, think tank funding, and war profiteering... His work has appeared in Responsible Statecraft, The Nation, The Intercept, The Brazilian Report, Drop Site, and The Hill."
He works for the institute Clifton cofounded.
He publishes in Drop Site — the outlet that launched with Hamas and pressed Khanna on October 7.
He publishes in The Nation, which launches the book.
He publishes in The Intercept, which Scahill cofounded.
Dahlia Scheindlin completes the panel. In Quincy's own words: "a public opinion researcher and a political advisor who has worked on nine national campaigns in Israel and in 15 other countries... a policy fellow at The Century Foundation... a senior analyst at Haaretz newspaper."
She supplies the Israeli voice — the same structural role Avraham Burg fills in the book's endorsements.

A panel on Israeli influence in America. Hosted by an institute one panelist cofounded. Moderated by that institute's own staffer. Promoting a book that panelist wrote.
No participant holds a contrary view.
This is not a debate. It is a launch.

What follows is not an argument about an argument. It is a record of a method.
The method is removal. Not persuasion, not rebuttal — the production of an authority sufficient to take a Jew off the air, off the panel, out of the room, without anyone having to engage a word she said.

In 2004 it took one magazine essay, cited by name in a petition, to put a thirty-year-old radio program before a governing board. In 2026 it takes a Washington think tank, a Simon & Schuster imprint, a national magazine, and a searchable database.
The venues escalate. The method does not change

THE CLAIM
The publisher's own description states that the lobby "launched an antisemitism witch hunt to suppress opponents rather than attempt to defend Israel's policies."
It states that the lobby "wields antisemitism as a legal and political weapon."
That claim is the point of this note. Not because it is new. Because it is not.

THE ENDORSEMENTS
Avraham Burg, former Speaker of the Knesset, endorses the book explicitly "as an Israeli and as a Jew."
In 2021, Independent Jewish Voices hosted a panel built around Burg's petition through the Israeli courts to have his own official designation as a Jew revoked.
John Mearsheimer writes that the lobby's success is "bad for the United States, bad for Israel, and bad for Jews all around the world."
Also endorsing: Stephen Walt, Mearsheimer's co-author on The Israel Lobby and US Foreign Policy. Benjamin Moser, author of Anti-Zionism. Juan Cole, University of Michigan. Rogers M. Smith, University of Pennsylvania. Ron Paul.

THE METHOD
Fear Inc. mapped funding to argue that opposition to Islamism was manufactured.
Israel's Lobby maps funding to argue that support for Israel is manufactured.
Cleveland-Stout describes his own research focus as "foreign influence, think tank funding, and war profiteering."
Fifteen years, two subjects, one technique: trace the money, and the position is thereby discredited.
Not argued against. Accounted for.

BRIAN KLUG
Brian Klug is a Senior Research Fellow in Philosophy at St Benet's Hall, Oxford, and a member of the Oxford Faculty of Philosophy.
On February 2, 2004, The Nation published his essay "The Myth of the New Anti-Semitism."
Four months later it was cited by name, as authoritative refutation, in the campaign to remove Feminist Magazine from KPFK. The petition's own words: "The reviewer totally refutes and rejects Chesler's claims."
The article has since been removed from thenation./com. It survives only in the Internet Archive.

Klug was associated with the launch of Independent Jewish Voices in the United Kingdom in 2007 and with the drafting of its founding declaration.

In 2016, B'nai Brith Canada published an investigation finding that Independent Jewish Voices' official Twitter and Facebook accounts had directed followers to Veterans Today — designated a white supremacist hate site by both the Anti-Defamation League and the Southern Poverty Law Center — for an article asserting that no more than one million Jews were killed by Nazi Germany, and characterizing modern antisemitism as a natural reaction to Israeli policies. The article was also promoted by Sid Shniad, IJV's co-chair and official spokesperson. A follower publicly identified it as Holocaust denial. IJV neither answered nor removed the link.

B'nai Brith CEO Michael Mostyn: "IJV is a Jewish fig leaf for neo-Nazis and antisemites of all stripes."
In 2021 Klug was a contributing author of the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism, which holds that BDS, characterizing Israel as an apartheid state, and advocacy for Palestinian self-determination do not constitute antisemitism.

The method. On November 8, 2013 — the eve of the 75th anniversary of Pogromnacht — Klug delivered the public lecture at the Jewish Museum Berlin.
He asked the audience to imagine a London bus. A religious Jew, Rabbi Cohen, is thrown off it five separate times. Each time the audience is asked to determine whether this was antisemitism.
In four of the five scenarios, the answer is no.
A Jewish woman, Mrs. Goldstein, watches from the back of the bus. When she perceives antisemitism, the lecture corrects her: "Mrs Goldstein, who is watching this scene from the back of the bus, smells antisemitism. She is wrong."
She is introduced in order to be wrong. She is wrong twice.
Where a case is unclear, Klug prescribes a procedure: examine "the literature they produce, their history, their membership, their political connections, and so on." He concedes "the evidence might be insufficient" and "we can be wrong."
The default is doubt. Certainty requires an investigation almost no one can conduct.
The lecture also renders the dispute as symmetrical: "Critics of Israel, crossing a line in the sand, find themselves accused of antisemitism. They react by accusing their accusers, alleging that the charge against them is nothing more than the machinations of 'the Israel lobby'. At once, this is seized upon as an antisemitic slur, which in turn is denounced as a Zionist smear."

The Jew reporting antisemitism and the person invoking the Israel lobby, placed on equal footing, in an unseemly circle.

And it closes by dissolving the category. Antisemitism, he says, "points beyond itself" — one dot among "numerous dots with different names."

The framework presumes that hatred of Jews operates on evidence and can therefore be audited for it.

It does not. The lecture's own material proves it. Wilhelm Marr. The Nuremberg laws. The yellow star pinned to Imre Kertész in 1944. None of it required a reason. None of it waited for one.

Antisemites need no reason. This framework demands that Jews supply one before they are believed. That is a burden nothing else carries.

What he actually argues. In "Unasking Europe's Jewish Question," published by the University of Notre Dame's Contending Modernities on September 16, 2021, Klug goes considerably further than saying anti-Zionism is permissible.
He argues that Zionism is a European ideology alien to Judaism itself.
Herzl "went wrong from the very beginning." Israel "is the last outpost of Europe." Zionism amounts to "the nationalization of Judaism." Britain's Chief Rabbi, who wrote that one can no more separate Zionism from Judaism than separate the City of London from Great Britain, is cited as evidence of how far mainstream Jewish thought has strayed.
Then the device: Klug imagines Moses composing Herzl's pamphlet in an Egyptian palace, finds the idea absurd, and concludes that "the spirit of Zionism could hardly be more antithetical to the spirit of the biblical Exodus, the story that lies at the heart of the identity of am Yisroel, the Jewish people."

An Oxford philosopher, using the Exodus — recited every Pesach, invoked in the liturgy daily — to rule that the position held by most Jews and by the Chief Rabbi of the United Kingdom falls outside the Jewish tradition.
He also writes that "as the Shoah led to the Nakba, the cost was transferred to the Palestinians," and that Palestinians pay "twice over" for Europe's treatment of Jews — first for antisemitic exclusion, then for "anti-antisemitic inclusion." "Heads they lose, tails they lose."

A word of my own here, since everything else in this piece is documentary.
The objection is not that Klug argues. Jews argue. It is what we do. The Babylonian Talmud runs 2,711 double-sided pages of recorded disagreement, studied aloud in a singsong, with questions, replies, and proofs each carrying their own tune, in rooms noisy with it. Rashi. Tosafot. Thousands of commentaries and supercommentaries across the centuries, each one adding rather than settling. Whole passages devoted to cases that could never occur, preserved because the reasoning is the point. Completing it once is a lifetime's achievement, and you begin again.

That is argument in good faith, inside a shared framework, among people bound to one another and to the text.

Klug's is not that. It is a ruling issued from outside about what the tradition permits, delivered to strip standing from the Jews who hold it.

And Jewish life is not spent on this in any case. It is Torah, mitzvot, Shabbat — the fixed obligations of a week and a year. The identity is not theorized. It is practiced. No one who keeps Shabbat requires an Oxford philosopher's framework to know what they are.
The framework was never built to be lived by. It was built to be cited.
And it was. The petition to remove Feminist Magazine did not argue that Chesler was wrong. It cited Klug and declared the matter settled: "The reviewer totally refutes and rejects Chesler's claims."

That is the function. Not a contribution to a debate — an authority produced to end one. A Jewish philosopher at Oxford, invoked by name so that a thirty-year-old program could be brought before a board without anyone having to engage a word of what it aired.
Twenty-two years later the same authority appears in a declaration, in a directory, and in the jacket copy of a book from a Simon & Schuster imprint. The citation does the work. The argument never has to be made.

THE INFRASTRUCTURE
In December 2025, a website appeared called Jewish House of Peace, at jhpeace./org. It describes itself as "the comprehensive directory of Jewish organizations and notable figures advocating for peace, justice, and human rights in Palestine." It claims 100+ organizations and 300+ figures. Brian Klug has a profile there.
Its stated purpose, in its own words: "To provide visual proof of two essential truths: Anti-Zionism is not anti-Semitism... Pro-Palestinian voices are not rare."
Its stated method: "We believe that 'seeing is believing'... If someone only sees one or two Jewish people supporting Palestine, they might mistakenly believe that Israel represents the entire Jewish nation. But if they visit this site and immediately see 80+ Jewish organizations and hundreds of famous figures standing for justice, they can see the truth for themselves."
Its published inclusion criteria: support for a one-state solution, ending "the colonial occupation," BDS, the belief that Israel bears primary responsibility for the lack of peace, anti-Zionism, and "recognizing and opposing the genocide in Gaza."
The site names no owner, no staff, no board, no funder. It states: "This is a project (not an organization)."
In 2004, this argument required a magazine essay to be cited by name in a petition.
In 2026 it has a searchable database.
THE ARGUMENT HAS BEEN ON THIS STATION SINCE THE SEVENTIES
The claim that a lobby controls American policy on Israel did not arrive at Pacifica with a 2026 book. It has aired there for close to fifty years.
In 1979, Pacifica in Berkeley produced a 48-minute radio documentary, "The Gun and the Olive Branch: The Palestine Liberation Organization," catalogued in the Pacifica Radio Archives as AZ0396. I located it in the archive in the course of this investigation.
The documentary is sympathetic to the PLO throughout. Its featured interviewee, speaking from Beirut, is Rashid Khalidi.
Pacifica's own narrator identifies him five times, in Pacifica's own words:
"Rashid Khalidi, interviewed in Beirut, is an official spokesperson for the Palestinian news service Wafa." (7:34)
"PLO spokesperson Rashid Khalidi." (11:45)
"Rashid Khalidi, official spokesperson for the PLO." (21:00)
"Rashid Khalidi, interviewed at the headquarters of the PLO in Beirut." (29:57)
"Rashid Khalidi is the leading spokesperson for the PLO news agency, Wafa." (32:51)
The scholar Martin Kramer sources the same Pacifica documentary, establishing that these identifications corroborate Thomas Friedman's 1982 identification of Khalidi in the New York Times as "a director of the Palestinian press agency, Wafa" — a report dismissed for years as erroneous.
On the content, per Kramer: Khalidi justifies attacks on civilians as legitimate reactions to disproportionate Israeli violence (14:00); outlines PLO strategy and history; claims the organization represents all Palestinians everywhere; and argues for a "secular democratic state" to replace Israel, which he calls a "magnanimous" offer.

A federally licensed, listener-funded American broadcaster produced a sympathetic documentary featuring an official spokesman of the Palestine Liberation Organization, identified as such by its own narrator, five times, in 1979.

THE DURATION
Four months after The Nation published Klug's essay, it was cited in a campaign to remove Feminist Magazine from KPFK 90.7 FM, Pacifica Radio's Los Angeles station.
The program's offense was an interview with Phyllis Chesler about antisemitism.
Chesler stated at Yale in September 2010 that she had been the first pro-Israel and pro-democracy feminist guest in that station's history.
The campaign ran for months.
Its call for signatures was posted to LA Indymedia on June 14, 2004, nineteen days after the broadcast, addressed to the KPFK Local Station Board. It carried eight organizers: Diana Barahona, Farah Davari, Donas John, Yael Korin, Carole LaFlamme, Karin Pally, Karen Pomer, Emma Rosenthal.
By December 8, 2004, the same letter carried thirty-six signatories with affiliations printed beside their names:
Diana Barahona — KPFK Listener
Farah Davari — SWANA Collective of KPFK
Donas John — PEN USA, Freedom to Write Committee
Yael Korin — Women in Black–LA
Carole LaFlamme — Women in Black–LA
Karin Pally — Women in Black–LA
Karen Pomer — Founder, The Rainbow Sisters Project
Jessica Hoffmann — former member, KPFK Women's Coalition
Emma Rosenthal — Café Intifada; The Writing Empowerment Project
Dylan Rodríguez — Dept. of Ethnic Studies, UC Riverside
Mary Hughes — Women in Black–LA; International Solidarity Movement
John P. Jones — KPFK Listener
Paul Hershfield — KPFK Listener
Hector Chavez — KPFK Listener
Leslie Hope — CODEPINK
Darius Sarrafi — KPFK Listener
Justin Shahbaz — KPFK Listener
Sheila Pinkel — KPFK Listener
Bernie Eisenberg — Women in Black–LA
Anne Dugaw — KPFK Listener
Marc Stuart — KPFK Listener
Sally Marr — Artist/Activist
Peter Dudar — Artist/Activist
Jack VanAken — Dogs of Now website
Michael Shahin — SWANA Collective
Ed Pearl — KPFK Local Station Board
Chris Cheung — KPFK Listener
Darren Kim — Women in Black–LA
Greta Berlin — Women in Black–LA; International Solidarity Movement
Nancy Halpern Ibrahim — Palestine Aid Society
Elana Golden — Women in Black–LA
Joanne Nagy — KPFK Listener
Helen Aragon — KPFK Listener
Bruce Moore — 35-year listener-subscriber
Ceil Sorensen — San Fernando Valley Greens; The Alliance
Jim Odling — KPFK Listener/Sponsor
Ed Pearl signed as a sitting member of KPFK's own Local Station Board.
A member of the governing body of a federally licensed station publicly demanded that his own board review a program for what it aired.

WHAT THE STATION DID
Feminist Magazine was a legacy program. At the time of the campaign it had been on KPFK's air for roughly thirty years. The petition's own authors acknowledged this — they wrote that the collective held "their precious weekly hour of airtime, which they have possessed for decades."
They demanded it be taken off anyway.
Not a correction. Not a right of reply. Not a rebuttal segment. The removal of a thirty-year-old program from the schedule of a federally licensed station, because it aired one interview about contemporary antisemitism.
The station let the campaign run for months.
The producers were required to give testimony before the Local Station Board to justify their program's continued existence. One of the people who signed the petition demanding that review sat on that board.
There was no HR department. There was no process. There was no finding, no adjudication, no statement from management defending the program's right to air what it aired.
At minimum five separate organized attempts were made to remove the show.
And this at a station whose founding Articles of Incorporation, written by Lewis Hill, committed it to "accurate, objective, comprehensive news" and to "lasting understanding between nations and individuals of all nations, races, creeds and colors." The board deleted Hill's anti-propaganda clause in 1971.
THE DOUBLE STANDARD IS THE FINDING
KPFK addresses discrimination continuously. Racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, Islamophobia, ableism, colonialism, incarceration, immigration enforcement — each has dedicated programming, recurring hosts, and institutional support across the Pacifica network.

One hour on antisemitism, in a thirty-year-old program, produced a months-long removal campaign, a board proceeding, and thirty-six initial signatures.

In the same period and since, the same station has aired Middle East in Focus, hosted for decades by a man who told a colleague in the studio hallway, after a program on the expulsion of a million Mizrahi and Sephardic Jews from Arab lands: "I heard your show on the way to the station. Every word of it was a lie."

It has aired Radio Intifada, founded by a co-founder of the US Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel, succeeded by another, which has platformed the international coordinator of Samidoun — designated by the United States and Canada as a fundraising front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

It airs Middle East Minute+, described on KPFK's own program page as "a joint project of KPFK & Jewish Voice for Peace," Monday through Friday.
No petition. No board review. No campaign.

WHAT THE SIGNATORIES DID NEXT
Karin Pally. Women in Black–LA contact and organizer, Israel Philharmonic boycott campaign at Disney Hall, January–February 2007. Free Gaza Movement Los Angeles spokeswoman, SS Liberty voyage, July 2008. Free Gaza spokeswoman, Israeli warship interception, January 2009. Contributing writer, Washington Report on Middle East Affairs, BDS advocacy, March 2010.
Karen Pomer. Women in Black–LA. Free Gaza Movement Los Angeles spokeswoman. Washington Report BDS contributor, 2010. Signatory, Jews for Palestinian Right of Return, 2013. Photographed marching with Estee Chandler of JVP-LA, July 30, 2017. Active with Jews for Palestinian Right of Return, March 2022.
Greta Berlin. Subsequently removed from the Free Gaza Movement for posting antisemitic content.
Mary Hughes. Signed the 2006 Israel Philharmonic letter for Women in Black–LA. Passenger on the first Free Gaza voyage, August 2008. Speaker at the 2018 Women's Rally for Ahed Tamimi, introduced by Karen Pomer.
Elana Golden. 2006 Israel Philharmonic letter signatory.
Emma Rosenthal. 2006 Israel Philharmonic letter signatory.
Farah Davari and Michael Shahin. SWANA Collective — the direct predecessor of Radio Intifada, still airing on KPFK.
Dylan Rodríguez. Later central to California's Liberated Ethnic Studies movement, mandatory for high school graduation statewide under AB 101, signed 2021. Founding collective member, Institute for the Critical Study of Zionism, 2023.
Carol Smith. Women in Black–LA and National Lawyers Guild Los Angeles.

WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS IS ESCALATION
In 2004 the argument moved through independent papers, town hall meetings, and email, to remove one hour of programming from one radio station.
The objection was never to the work. The work was valued. The career advanced for twenty-three years.
The objection was to a Jew who lived as most Jews do and would not sell that out.
The price of not selling it out was, eventually, the platform itself.

That is not one person's story. The people who would answer this argument have, over the same twenty-two years, lost the platforms from which they once had — across journalism, the arts, and the academy. Jews who hold the ordinary positions most Jews hold have found the room narrowing. Jews who supply the argument have found it opening.

Clearing the ground is not a side effect of the campaign. It is the mechanism by which an argument this weak has gone twenty-two years without a serious public answer.

The signatories were listeners signing a letter.
Within two years, the same names appear on a boycott campaign against an Israeli orchestra.
Within four, they are spokeswomen for a flotilla attempting to breach a naval blockade, and passengers aboard it.
By 2010, they are publishing BDS advocacy.
By 2013, signing for the right of return.
By 2017 and 2018, marching and speaking alongside the host who now holds the airtime the 2004 campaign sought to clear.
The institutions moved with them. The SWANA Collective that signed became Radio Intifada, still on KPFK. Dylan Rodríguez moved from a signature on a listener petition to a graduation requirement for every public high school student in California.
And the argument itself moved from a magazine essay to a hardcover from a Simon & Schuster imprint — endorsed by a former Speaker of the Knesset and two endowed chairs, launched across a Washington think tank and that same magazine, promoted by writers whose bylines run through an outlet that debuted by publishing Hamas at length and that asked a member of Congress to call October 7 justified.
Nothing here dissolved. Nothing moderated.
Each stage supplied the personnel, the argument, and the institutional weight for the next.

The airtime was cleared. It stayed cleared.

That is what the method is for.

I am documenting how, not why. The record is public, dated, and drawn from these institutions' own published words. 
Signed, Unwaiverhesed
From my research

text:
2010, Laszlo Hanyecz pays 10,000 Bitcoin for two Papa John’s pizzas - the most expensive food order in history. today, those same coins are worth roughly $645 million. at Bitcoin’s 2025 peak, they crossed $1.2 billion.

May 22, 2010. Bitcoin has no exchange, no price chart, nothing beyond a handful of programmers on a forum. it takes five days for anyone to accept Hanyecz’s offer. a 19-year-old in California, Jeremy Sturdivant, finally takes the trade - orders two pizzas, has them sent to Florida.

“I paid for a pizza in Bitcoins.”

the exchange becomes Bitcoin’s first real-world commercial transaction, now marked every year as Bitcoin Pizza Day.

neither man held onto the coins. Hanyecz spent them. Sturdivant, the one who actually received all 10,000 BTC, didn’t keep them either.

two people touched the most expensive pizza order in history. neither one of them still owns a slice of it.

text:
summer 2007, a Citadel partner takes a Sunday morning call from a co-head of Sowood Capital. Sowood has just lost hundreds of millions of dollars and needs to unload almost its entire portfolio before Monday’s open.

Citadel assembles a 50-person team within hours. eight people fly to Boston that same day to run due diligence on the book.

a competing bank is bidding on the same portfolio. by that night, its senior banker is done for the day.

“he said, look, it’s getting late, this isn’t gonna get done tonight. I’m heading off to bed, I’m telling my guys to go home, and we’ll pick this up in the morning.”

“and I said, there will be nothing to pick up in the morning. we’re going to get this done. he sort of laughed and hung up.”

6AM, before the markets open, Citadel owns the entire portfolio - roughly $30 billion, absorbed overnight.

Ken Griffin closes the story on a line he credits to President Lincoln - good things come to those who wait, but only what’s left behind by those who hustle.

the offer never came back around in the morning. neither did the other banker’s night off.

text:
Three U.S. states could lose a fifth of their water from the Colorado River.
A proposed federal plan would require Arizona, California and Nevada to reduce their use of the drought-stricken Colorado River by 21 percent in 2027 and 2028, according to a senior state water official who spoke to Reuters.
The Lower Basin states would contribute a combined 3.2 million acre-feet of water to the river system over the two years. One acre-foot equals about 326,000 gallons (1.2 million liters), enough to cover an acre of land with one foot of water.
The reductions could become much deeper after 2028.
From 2029 through 2036, the three states could be required to cut as much as 3 million acre-feet every year to keep Lake Mead and Lake Powell above critical levels. The plan would be reviewed every two years as conditions change.
The Colorado River supplies water to roughly 40 million people, irrigates farmland responsible for around 15 percent of U.S. food production and fills reservoirs that generate electricity for more than 6 million people.
But decades of drought, rising temperatures and heavy demand have left the system severely depleted. Federal officials said in April that Colorado River reservoirs held only about 36 percent of their total capacity after the lowest winter snowpack on record.
The seven states that rely on the river have spent three years negotiating new rules to replace the current agreement, which expires at the end of 2026.
Arizona, California and Nevada have offered major reductions, but they want Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming to cut their use as well.
The Upper Basin states argue they already receive less water during dry years and that the Lower Basin, which consumes most of the river’s water, should make the deeper reductions.
The Bureau of Reclamation has not yet formally adopted the plan. A final federal decision could trigger lawsuits if the states cannot agree, potentially extending uncertainty over one of America’s most important water sources.

text:
🏈 So who is this kid Terry Mclaurin is mentoring? 🏈

Jaden Bradley, UDFA WR was a bit of late bloomer who transferred from Pitt to Charlotte to UNLV. 

In 2025 he had a breakout season at UNLV, he posted:
- 58 receptions, 931 yards, 16.1 yards per catch,4 TDs
-Was second Team All Mountain West. Also, contributed on special teams, punt block returned for a TD, kick returns. 

His Measurables (Pro Day)
- Height: 6’3”
- Weight: 203 lbs
- Arms: 31.5” / Hands: 9.25”
- 40 yard: 4.57
- Vertical: 36”
- Broad jump: 10’5”
- Shuttle: 4.25 / 3-Cone: 7.10
- RAS of 7.91 (A pretty solid athletic profile for a big receiver)

What the Scouting Reports say:

Strengths:  
- Excellent size and length to win contested catches and 50/50 balls  
- Strong hands, good body control and ball tracking  
- A long strider with deceptive top end speed  
- Physical at the catch point  
- Proven special teams value

Weaknesses/Areas to develop:  
- Route suddenness and polish (is not the twitchiest separator)  
- Being able consistently create separation vs NFL corners
- Timing and details (This is exactly what Terry McLaurin has been coaching to him)

Is he a fit with the Commanders? 

In David Blough’s offense he wants receivers who can create mismatches. Bradley offers:
- A size advantage for red zone and outside work
- A bigger target for QB 
- Has a special teams value that helps find paths on a roster in thin WR rooms  

Terry McLaurin has repeatedly praised his “pro like feel” and called him a sponge who’s been soaking up every detail on releases, hand placement, and red zone technique. This is the kind of developmental, high upside piece you want a veteran like Terry working with. He is a long shot to make the final 53, but could be a guy who starts his career off on the practice squad. Or you never know? Maybe the next Adam Thielan. 😂

Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").

Sako

In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
