Years of reported brain injuries linked to a Six Flags roller coaster | CNN

In the span of less than a week this July, surgeons at a Southern California hospital raced to save the lives of two women suffering from alarmingly similar brain hemorrhages.

The severe injuries were the kind doctors encounter in patients after high-speed collisions or other violent accidents that cause the brain to twist and slam inside one’s skull.

Neither woman, however, had been involved in a crash, fall or other such incident.

Instead, they had ridden an extreme roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain, known as X2, which draws thrill-seekers from around the world with its rotating seats, near-vertical drops and unpredictable movements. It has long been the park’s marquee attraction — promoted as a “[rite] of passage for the ultimate daredevil.”

But behind the ride’s legendary reputation lies a troubling record of serious injuries, a CNN investigation has found.

X2 has been linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries and hospitalizations over nearly two decades, a review of medical records, depositions and legal filings shows. Among the casualties are riders who suffered life-altering disabilities, fell into comas and two who died of their injuries. Park officials, meanwhile, have long fielded scores of complaints about other head and neck injuries sustained after riding the attraction, according to internal records cited by an expert witness for a plaintiff in court filings.

Yet despite years of warnings from the park’s visitors, attorneys and medical experts about the perils of riding X2, officials at the theme park – located in Valencia, California – and state regulators allowed the attraction to continue operating.

“I personally don’t think head injury should be an expected risk from going on a roller coaster ride, and there is no reason a ride can’t be properly designed to prevent injuries like this,” said Lyndia Wu, a mechanical engineering professor at the University of British Columbia who has researched the effects of roller coasters on the brain.

According to research by Wu and others, the risk of traumatic brain injuries associated with roller coasters is considered to be very low, though much of this research dates back many years and Wu told CNN there may be higher-risk rides that need to be further investigated, such as X2. Some high-profile cases from other attractions have involved those with suspected pre-existing conditions, such as a woman who died after riding the Goliath roller coaster at the same Six Flags location in 2001 when an aneurysm ruptured in her brain.

What makes X2 different from other roller coasters is its 4th-dimensional quality — meaning its seats are rotating 360 degrees around the track as trains reach speeds of nearly 80 miles per hour for roughly two minutes. There are only two other such roller coasters in the world: One in China, and the other in Japan, which closed temporarily last year after a fatal injury involving a park worker inspecting the ride.

Six Flags closed the roller coaster the evening of July 12, according to a spokesperson. This was nearly a full day after the latest injury there, and park officials have remained silent about what necessitated the closure.

The California Division of Occupational Safety and Health, which oversees amusement park ride operations, did not respond to questions about the history of brain injuries allegedly associated with X2 and did not say how it has deemed it safe to reopen after past incidents. It would only say an inspection remains ongoing.

Six Flags also declined to answer detailed questions from CNN, including questions about why X2 remained operational in the wake of the first July injury, saying the only information it is sharing is that “the ride remains closed at this time.”

Attorneys for the theme park have defended the roller coaster in court when sued by riders or their families over injuries, arguing that a sign warns passengers that “there are inherent risks in the participation in or on any amusement ride or attraction.” They have also said X2 is regularly tested and that the physical forces riders experience are not strong enough to create a traumatic brain injury for a “normal” rider using it “as instructed.”

Three neurosurgeons who have treated the two women injured in July disagreed.

“In our professional opinion,” the surgeons wrote in an email reviewed by CNN, “the severe brain injuries requiring emergent neurosurgical attention were the result of a traumatic rapid acceleration-deceleration event experienced while on the X2 ride.”

Troubles from the start

The groundbreaking attraction, which Six Flags has sunk millions of dollars into, was plagued with problems from the outset.

Construction of X2 plunged its maker, Arrow Dynamics, into bankruptcy after the company miscalculated costs, according to a trade publication at the time, and the roller coaster – initially called X – opened months behind schedule in January 2002. Six Flags redesigned it in 2007, but even when it reopened as X2 a year later, it was frequently out of operation.

None of this, however, stopped roller coaster enthusiasts from around the world from traveling to Magic Mountain for a chance to experience the first-of-its kind ride.

“X2 has been one of the most popular thrill rides on the planet,” Six Flags boasted on YouTube in 2014. “On ordinary roller coasters, the train stays in line with the track…but there is nothing ordinary about X2.”

Mounting reports of injuries

In September 2014, Selena O’Neill, 17, knew something was wrong as soon as she got off X2 with friends. Her head ached and she struggled to see and walk straight.

Her right leg began shaking any time she stood up and pointed outward in an unusual position, and when her grandmother took her to the doctor the next day, she suffered a seizure during the appointment, according to court records. Doctors examining the previously healthy teenager at a Los Angeles hospital discovered a subdural hematoma, a life-threatening injury which occurs when blood collects on the surface of the brain. They directly attributed it to the ride.

O’Neill sued the theme park in 2015. But her injuries drew little public attention, and it’s unclear if they were ever reported to state authorities. State regulators did not comment on this when asked by CNN.

Internal Six Flags records obtained by O’Neill’s attorney during the lawsuit show at least five riders had visited the hospital complaining of head pain prior to O’Neill’s injury. Her attorney also pointed to a prior lawsuit filed by a 62-year-old man who had suffered a traumatic brain injury after riding X2 with his two daughters in 2009, years before O’Neill ever boarded the attraction.

Hospital physicians would later detail her case in a 2019 medical journal article without naming X2. The doctors warned that “advances of roller-coaster technology and industry competition for thrill-seeking patrons may ultimately improve acceleration and performance beyond the passenger’s physical ability to tolerate them.”

The case was closed in 2017, and Six Flags argued in court filings that O’Neill should have been aware of potential risks when she chose to board. O’Neill requested that her case be dismissed after settling with the maker of X2’s vehicles, according to court filings.

As reports of serious head injuries mounted, longtime riders of X2 took to internet forums to question the aging coaster’s increasingly jarring experience and give advice on how riders could brace themselves to avoid a concussion.

Many reported the worst jolts to the head coming near the end.

“It honestly felt like a boxer punched me in the head twice,” one rider on Reddit wrote back in 2018, proceeding to offer a “defensive riding recommendation” to others braving X2: “Holding your head back against the rest makes it even worse so do not attempt this. Instead, as the ride nears the last two maneuvers lean forward as far as you can to try to avoid or mitigate the impact. You will get some mild whiplash, but it is better.”

For Sheila Katerelos, then 50, X2 was the second ride of the day during a visit to Six Flags in February 2020. In a court deposition, she described feeling a “sharp, throbbing pain” when her head slammed the back of the headrest. The pain, she said, reached a 10 out of 10 by the time the she pulled back into the station.

Katerelos became nauseated and dizzy while waiting in line for another ride and her husband, a doctor, became concerned as he witnessed her move increasingly slowly, drag one of her legs and slur her words. He immediately drove her to the emergency room where she was hospitalized for five days and diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury and multiple subdural hematomas, according to court records.

Katerelos’ lawsuit against the company that makes X2’s trains is currently awaiting trial.

A year later, in 2021, Lucy Alvarez, a 46-year-old phlebotomist, had a similar experience when she visited the amusement park with her sister, according to medical records and her attorney. She said she felt so dizzy that she had to sit down. She knew she had hit the back of her head hard on the ride’s headrest, but she figured the pain would get better, so she headed back to San Diego. When her light-headedness and head pain still hadn’t gone away nine days later, she went to the emergency room, where she was diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury – specifically a traumatic subdural hematoma – due to the roller coaster ride, medical records show.

After the injury, her headaches and mental fogginess made it difficult to focus, her attorney told CNN, and she was unable to complete nursing school. She still struggles with memory loss, balance issues and chronic migraines, the attorney said.

In response to her allegations, Six Flags said in a legal filing that any injuries that occurred were due to Alvarez’s own negligence and reiterated its argument that passengers are agreeing to assume risk. Her attorney told CNN a trial is scheduled for October 2027.

College grad dies hours after X2

Christopher Hawley, a 22-year-old recent college graduate, rode X2 in June of 2022 with his cousin and brother. According to court records, the three of them hit their heads multiple times on the back of the seat as they were flipped like “rag dolls.”

Shortly after exiting, Hawley complained of feeling lightheaded before slumping to the ground and going unconscious. “I will never forget the fear from the look he gave me as his eyes closed,” his cousin testified in a court deposition.

Hawley was transported to nearby Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital where surgeons discovered brain bleeding so severe it was squeezing his brain towards one side of his skull, according to court records.

By the time surgeons opened his skull, Hawley’s brain had swollen so intensely it began bulging out of the opening they made in an attempt to relieve the pressure. Hawley, an aspiring actor, had been in excellent health when he boarded X2, according to court records. He died less than ten hours later.

The neurosurgeon who treated Hawley likened his injuries to those sustained by “shaken baby syndrome,” and the medical examiner ruled his death had been caused by blunt head trauma from “a park ride accident,” according to the coroner’s report.

And the theme park’s internal records showed it had fielded at least 70 prior head and neck injury complaints from X2 riders in the three years leading up to Hawley’s death, according to a declaration by an expert hired by Hawley’s family, who reviewed the records.

It’s unclear how closely Six Flags tracks injuries and the theme park successfully fought in court to keep the first aid and medical incident reports under seal, arguing to a judge their disclosure “will serve only to fuel sensational media coverage portraying the X2 ride as dangerous, thereby tainting the jury pool.”

In an interview with CNN, a Colorado woman who posted about her experience on Reddit said she reported symptoms of a concussion to the park last year – along with other injuries her family members had experienced from X2. But park officials never addressed her report or checked on their wellbeing, said the woman, who is a nationwide passholder and asked to remain anonymous to avoid retribution from Six Flags.

Records show that Hawley’s was the second death linked to the ride. In 2010, a 28-year-old single mother, Hilda Farias, died after riding X2. Medical experts at the time suspected her death was caused by a brain abnormality that ruptured because of the intensity of the ride. A suit by her family settled for an undisclosed amount, according to court filings.

Following Hawley’s death in 2022, state officials told Six Flags to immediately shut down X2 and leave it in its current condition so it could be inspected.

Within days, the state allowed the park to reopen the roller coaster. But according to records reviewed during a deposition of the park’s director of maintenance, state officials were allegedly unaware that maintenance workers had replaced a wheel on one of the train cars prior to their inspection.

State officials did not appear to interview any witnesses or medical experts as part of their inspection of the ride. Instead, as is typical under state regulations, the inspector relied on safety and testing data provided by Six Flags that showed X2 had once again met safety standards adopted by the state.

Those standards, however, were developed by a committee that includes ride manufacturers and theme park operators.

Brian Avery, a professor at the University of Florida who specializes in ride safety and risk management, told CNN these standards are a good starting point but do not account for real-world factors such as the movement of a rider’s head, where the rider is seated, and whether the rider’s head hits the back of the seat.

Avery, who has worked as an expert witness on behalf of both riders and theme parks but has not been involved in an X2 case, said that repeated traumatic brain injuries linked to the same ride “constitute a clear safety signal” that should justify a comprehensive review of the ride.

Hawley’s parents sued the theme park in 2023, and Six Flags argued in court that the ride falls within approved industry standards and that its forces were not strong enough to cause a hematoma. The case was scheduled to go to trial in September, but court records show that it settled on Wednesday.

‘It’s got to stop’

The last thing Hawaii resident Pamela Guillen, 40, clearly remembers about riding X2 this July was how anxious she was about getting on the iconic roller coaster her daughter so desperately wanted them to experience together. She told herself it would be the last ride of the day, it would be over in a matter of minutes and then she and her family would go get a nice dinner to celebrate her daughter’s 16th birthday, Guillen told CNN.

But as she dipped and swerved, Guillen hit her head multiple times on the headrest, according to ambulance records that show when her car pulled back into the station, she had to be escorted from her seat and began vomiting. Her daughter Camille Marquez recounted how her mother’s eyes and mouth were open as if she was in shock from the intensity of the ride.

Guillen lost consciousness as soon as she sat down on a bench, ambulance records show, and paramedics arrived to find her unresponsive, with her pupils looking unequal and “sluggish.”

“Mommy, please wake up,” Marquez remembers telling her mother. “I kept rubbing her thigh and kept shaking her to wake up and she wouldn’t.”

Guillen was placed on a ventilator in the back of an ambulance. A CT scan revealed a severe subdural hematoma and brain compression, so doctors at the hospital intubated her and took her straight into the operating room, medical records show.

Guillen’s family waited anxiously as the same surgical team who treated Hawley four years before removed part of Guillen’s skull to release the pressure on her brain.

When Guillen woke up in a hospital bed two weeks later with her head shaved and about 20 staples in her scalp, she had no idea what had happened to her. She could only say one word at a time at first.

“You go in as yourself, and then when you come back, you’re a medical emergency. Like I still can’t wrap my head around that,” Guillen said. “There’s a difference between being jerked around and brain damage.”

Guillen described slowly learning how to talk and walk again and says she battles terrible headaches and brain fog and needs medication to prevent seizures.

“I’m very lucky to be alive,” she said. “I’m taking it a day at a time to not overwhelm myself and to not go into a dark hole of mourning who I was and what I was able to do before this.”

Six Flags did not respond to CNN’s inquiries about whether park officials notified the state of the incident, or if it closed the ride after Guillen’s injury. According to Guillen’s daughter, no representative from Six Flags has reached out to the family since initially offering them food the night of her injury.

Six days later, 25-year-old Los Angeles resident Naomi Greer-Wilkinson boarded X2 during a day at the park with her twin brother and younger sister. Just like Guillen, she lost consciousness shortly after riding the roller coaster and was rushed to the hospital for emergency brain surgery, according to her family.

Greer-Wilkinson’s parents told CNN they were informed by doctors their daughter had suffered a severe traumatic brain injury and they should prepare for the worst.

“Naomi should have never ever in a million years even had the option to get on that ride,” said her mother, Artemis Greer.

Whoever made the decision to keep X2 operational last month has “a lot to answer for,” said Greer-Wilkinson’s father, Joshua Wilkinson. “It’s got to stop.”

Greer remains in critical condition in a coma, hooked up to a ventilator and feeding tube that are keeping her alive. “This is the hardest thing a human being could go through,” her mother said of watching her daughter – whom she described as “wise for her age,” hilarious and kind.

“This is cruel,” she added.

A representative from Six Flags offered the family food from McDonald’s when Greer-Wilkinson first arrived in the emergency room, according to her mother. But they haven’t heard anything since.

Bitcoin’s payment history is full of moments that look completely unhinged in hindsight.

Here are five of the wildest historic examples of it actually being used to buy real things.

1. Two Papa John’s pizzas for 10,000 BTC (May 22, 2010)
 Programmer Laszlo Hanyecz posted on Bitcointalk offering 10,000 bitcoin for two large pizzas. Jeremy Sturdivant took him up on it, ordered from Papa John’s, and delivered them. At the time the coins were worth roughly $41. That single transaction is widely recognized as the first real-world commercial purchase with Bitcoin. Hanyecz kept the offer open for months and later said he spent tens of thousands more BTC on pizza that year. Those original 10,000 coins are now worth well over a billion dollars. Bitcoin Pizza Day is still celebrated every May 22.

2. Alpaca wool socks for 75 BTC a pair (February 2011)
 A small family farm in Haydenville, Massachusetts—Grass Hill Alpacas—became one of the first merchants to accept Bitcoin after the owner’s son convinced his parents. They charged 75 BTC per pair of socks (Bitcoin was still under a dollar). Orders came in from around the world; even lead developer Gavin Andresen bought some. Within months the price of Bitcoin rose so fast they slashed the sock price to 5 BTC. Those original 75-BTC pairs would later be worth millions. The humble alpaca became an unofficial early Bitcoin mascot.

3. Crossing the United States living only on Bitcoin (April–June 2011)
 A Bitcoiner known as Plato (TheRealPlato) drove from Connecticut to California without spending a single U.S. dollar. Bitcoin was around $1–$2 and almost no businesses accepted it. He relied on forum members, in-person trades, and people willing to buy him gas or food and accept BTC in return. He documented the trip on a blog and Twitter using the hashtag #BitcoinRoadTrip. It was one of the earliest real-world tests of whether Bitcoin could function as actual money when almost nobody treated it that way.

4. WikiLeaks surviving a financial blockade with Bitcoin donations (June 2011)
 After WikiLeaks published classified U.S. diplomatic cables, Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, and others cut off donations, wiping out an estimated 95% of its revenue. The organization started accepting Bitcoin. Satoshi Nakamoto publicly warned that the attention could be dangerous for the still-tiny network (“WikiLeaks has kicked the hornet’s nest”). Donations still flowed—more than 4,000 BTC over the following years. It became one of the first high-profile demonstrations that Bitcoin could work as censorship-resistant money when traditional payment rails were shut down.

5. A Hawaiian flight attendant buys a ticket to space with 350 BTC (November 2013)
 Richard Branson announced that Virgin Galactic would accept Bitcoin for its $250,000 suborbital flights. The first customer was a flight attendant from Hawaii who paid the full fare in bitcoin—about 350 BTC at the time. Branson converted the coins to dollars immediately to lock in the price. It was the first known purchase of a spaceflight ticket with cryptocurrency and a surreal snapshot of how quickly some early holders were willing to spend their coins on once-in-a-lifetime experiences.

These were creative, small-scale, often improvised payments that happened when Bitcoin was still a curiosity.

But the important thing is this: the payments settled on an immutable ledger that’s verified by the public and no intermediary was required.

text:
FDA Clears First-of-Its-Kind Nonmedication Treatment for PTSD | Texas A&M University

The FDA has cleared a system that uses brain activity data to personalize magnetic stimulation for PTSD, adding a new nonmedication treatment option.

Every day in the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide, while 7% of veterans are diagnosed each year with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Against this backdrop, researchers at Texas A&M Health are helping advance a more personalized approach to treating PTSD.

A system developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with the research team of Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology recently received FDA clearance. The technology maps brain activity associated with PTSD and uses those measurements to personalize treatment. The clinical findings are still being prepared for public dissemination, but preliminary results reported by the company suggest substantial improvements in PTSD symptoms.

PTSD can develop after exposure to events that go beyond ordinary stress, including combat, accidents, natural disasters, or other forms of violence. About 6% of people develop PTSD symptoms during their lifetimes, with substantially higher rates among women and veterans.

Since PTSD became an official diagnosis in 1980, common treatments have included talk therapy and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) medications, such as sertraline and fluoxetine. These approaches, however, do not work for everyone.

A 2020 review of PTSD medications found that although some patients improved, many did not. Self-reported symptom scores improved by 6.8 to 10.1 points, while remission rates reached no more than 10.9%.

Personalized brain stimulation showed stronger trial results

Wave Neuroscience reported substantially stronger preliminary outcomes from its clinical trial, according to chief medical officer Erik Won, DO.

“In comparison to that study, our FDA trial reported a 52% reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” Won said. “And more importantly, we saw 68% remission in our clinical trial. So, it’s really a quantum change, an inflection point in what we can offer to patients. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.”

The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), combines an electroencephalogram (EEG), which measures electrical activity in the brain, with transcranial magnetic stimulation. TMS, already used for other mental health conditions, delivers magnetic pulses through a coil placed against the scalp.

“Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, was previously FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression,” Won said. “By adding an augmented AI-derived multivariate algorithm, we were able to personalize protocols that received FDA clearance for post-traumatic stress disorder, which should open up market access to about 13 million people who may be struggling with PTSD.”

That individualized targeting is central to MeRT.

Treatment is tailored to each brain

Ramos, a physician scientist with decades of experience in precision medicine, studies treatments designed around the characteristics of an individual patient and condition rather than using the same approach for everyone.

“Most clinical interventions for the treatment of PTSD do not work very well,” Ramos said. “So, this is a huge area where identifying interventions that could hopefully add quality of life to the people impacted by this disorder would be tremendously impactful.”

Fred Walke, chief executive officer of Wave Neuroscience, said Ramos’s expertise in precision medicine made him a natural collaborator for the study.

Traditional TMS generally uses a more standardized protocol, Ramos explained, whereas MeRT adjusts treatment according to the individual brain.

Humans are about 99.9% genetically alike, but the remaining 0.1% can have important effects. By personalizing treatment to each participant, the researchers were able to target individual brain activity patterns and observed significant reductions in PTSD symptom severity.

Ramos compared the difference to repairing a leaking roof. Standard TMS, he said, resembles placing a tarp over the leak to manage the symptoms, while MeRT is intended to be more targeted, like replacing damaged shingles and addressing the source of the problem.

FDA clearance followed an accelerated path

MeRT’s path toward FDA clearance began in 2024, when it received an FDA breakthrough design designation, according to Dr. Rick Silva, executive director of clinical trials at the Institute of Biosciences and Technology.

The designation can accelerate FDA review by reducing some administrative delays while still requiring the technology to meet scientific and medical standards.

Completing the final stages of FDA review remains a lengthy and demanding process.

Silva said this project was particularly rewarding because it began during the COVID-19 pandemic and reached FDA clearance unusually quickly. Medical device clinical trials often take about a decade to complete and secure clearance, he said, whereas this process took just over two years.

He credited the Wave Neuroscience team with the expertise needed to meet the scientific and regulatory demands of the project.

“I’ve been involved in probably close to 1,000 projects in academic medical centers over the years at varying degrees of depth and detail,” Silva said. “Patients are why I do what I do. It’s hard, and the failure rate is high, and it’s a lot of work. But when you get to a point where something is going to benefit patients, it’s very professionally gratifying and personally gratifying in many ways as well.”

PTSD gains a nonmedication treatment option

For Dr. Israel Liberzon, distinguished professor in psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, the clearance adds a different kind of option to PTSD care.

Liberzon, who served as the study’s lead psychiatrist and PTSD expert, said that once available to patients, MeRT will be the only FDA-cleared nonmedication treatment option specifically for PTSD.

“Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” Liberzon said. “It doesn’t mean that only two of them are used, but both are SSRIs. This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety-provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.”

Participants in the MeRT clinical trial received five sessions each week for five to six weeks. The beneficial effects appeared to continue after treatment ended.

“People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.”

Won said the technology could eventually be explored for other conditions, including depression and anxiety.

Dr. Leslie S. Prichep, chief scientific officer of Wave Neuroscience, said the clearance builds on decades of research into electrical brain activity and personalized intervention.

“The FDA clearance of the MeRT System reflects decades of scientific research using electrophysiological biomarkers in identifying abnormal brain activity profiles and guiding personalized intervention strategies,” Prichep said. “We believe this represents an important advancement toward a more objective, data-informed model of mental healthcare.”

Walke said he hopes a more individualized and objectively guided approach can also reduce stigma surrounding mental health treatment by making it resemble treatment for other physical conditions.

“One of the goals of the company is to create a platform for mental healthcare that uses objective imagery to help patients understand why they’re experiencing life the way that they are,” Walke said. “That insight, compounded with proven technologies, promises incredibly high efficacy when personalized.”

Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are also working with stakeholders to expand access and make treatment affordable through insurance coverage.

“Our hope is that this research and technology can be a catalyst for more widespread development and innovation of more effective, personalized and precision-guided treatments,” Won said. “This is proof positive that population-scale personalized medicine is not just an aspirational goal but is an achievable reality today.”

The MeRT effort brings together researchers and clinicians across several disciplines with the goal of reducing the burden of PTSD. FDA clearance moves the technology closer to broader patient use.

“Texas A&M has a very rich history of military and veteran priorities,” Ramos said. “It’s a no-brainer that Texas A&M faculty would be interested in and supportive of an initiative that hopefully would bring positive solutions to a big problem. And anything we could do to help alleviate that problem is going to go a long way towards making a difference in the individual’s life as well as the people who are close to them. I feel very fortunate that we at Texas A&M were meaningfully involved in this project.”

text:
Forty-seven states settled mid-trial. Texas passed on joining, then cut its own cheque. The side deal is larger than every state's share but California's, and Texas never sued in Oakland.

Ryan Autullo at Bloomberg Law reports that a week before the $17 billion multistate deal, Texas was offered a chance to join. It passed.

Texas worked up a $1.05 billion side deal with Meta that maxes at $1.335 billion if YouTube and TikTok agree to the same terms and safety changes Meta accepted in the multistate settlement.

Details sit in an Aug 25 email exchange between Brent Webster, first assistant to Texas AG Ken Paxton, and Meta CLO C.J. Mahoney, obtained by Bloomberg Law.

The payout is larger than every state but California, which gets up to $2.2 billion. California helped orchestrate the 29-state federal suit. Texas never joined that case, never appeared in Oakland, never sued Meta on its own in that action.

Webster told Bloomberg Law the multistate deal "was not as good for Texas as we wanted." Texas's share would have been "significantly less." He declined to reveal the proposed amount.

Meta settled mid-trial after the case started Aug 18 in the Northern District of California. Tennessee walked into the multistate deal at up to $739 million. New Mexico, sitting on a judgment above $900 million, did not join. Florida AG James Uthmeier called the amount "peanuts" and committed to trial.

No other state negotiated outside Wednesday's announcement.

Texas previously took $1.4 billion from Meta on facial recognition in July 2024, and $1.375 billion from Google on privacy. Those had outside-counsel cuts. This addiction side deal was in-house, so the proceeds stay with the state.

Paxton personally negotiated with Meta executives, Webster said. Meta global policy head Kevin Martin thanked Paxton "for his leadership in protecting Texas teens and making this standard possible."

Webster said after Meta, the priority is a TikTok trial set Oct 12 in Travis County.

I would start with the state that never showed up in Oakland.

text:
To satisfy both cattle physiology (thermal neutrality of 5°C to 20°C, low-to-moderate humidity, avoidance of extreme heat/mud) and the biological requirement for year-round natural grass growth, the ideal climate is an Oceanic / Temperate Maritime Climate (Köppen Cfb / Csb). [1, 2] 
These regions rarely experience sustained sub-freezing winters (which stop plant growth) or oppressive summer heat waves and high humidity (which trigger heat stress). [1, 2] 
------------------------------
## 1. [New Zealand](https://t.co/UAtQou5B2K) ([Waikato](https://t.co/bBqqyF9OZT), [Taranaki](https://t.co/2EyVxjXc8j), [Southland](https://t.co/pyc24AdUKm))

* 
* Climate profile: Cool-temperate maritime (Cfb).
* Why it fits: Temperatures consistently sit between 8°C and 22°C year-round with reliable rainfall. Cattle rarely face thermal or severe cold stress, and pastures can sustain vegetative growth or stockpiling throughout winter. [1, 3] 
* 

## 2. [Ireland](https://t.co/NTYKTnTTyu) and Coastal United Kingdom

* 
* Climate profile: Hyper-oceanic temperate (Cfb).
* Why it fits: The North Atlantic Drift keeps winter temperatures mild (typically 4°C–9°C) and summer temperatures cool (15°C–20°C). [Ireland](https://t.co/NTYKTnTTyu) boasts one of the longest natural grass-growing seasons globally.
* Management note: Well-drained soils are necessary to manage heavy winter precipitation and avoid hoof-damaging mud. [2] 
* 

## 3. Pampas of Argentina & [Uruguay](https://t.co/bHfiVzzfIu)

* 
* Climate profile: Humid subtropical to temperate maritime (Cfa/Cfb).
* Why it fits: Long known for grass-fed beef systems, winters are very mild without persistent snow cover, allowing perennial grasses to produce or remain grazeable through winter.
* Management note: Peak summer months can briefly push cattle into the heat stress zone (>25°C), requiring shade management.
* 

## 4. [Pacific Northwest](https://t.co/q2404pvgk4) & Northern California Coast (US) / Southern Chile

* 
* Climate profile: Mediterranean / Oceanic coastal (Csb/Cfb).
* Why it fits: Coastal fog and maritime winds keep summer temperatures well below dangerous heat thresholds, while ocean currents prevent severe winter freezes, allowing cool-season grasses (fescues, orchardgrass, rye) to grow nearly 365 days a year.
* 

## 5. Southeastern Coastal Australia & [Tasmania](https://t.co/gHL7qQG0IW)

* 
* Climate profile: Temperate maritime.
* Why it fits: [Tasmania](https://t.co/gHL7qQG0IW) and coastal [Victoria](https://t.co/JhTQWVmrez) offer cool summer grazing and mild winters with minimal frost, eliminating the need for indoor winter housing or heavy supplemental grain feeding.
* 

------------------------------

| Region | Primary Advantage | Main Climatic Challenge |
|---|---|---|
| New Zealand[](https://t.co/UAtQou5B2K) | Highest natural pasture productivity per hectare | Soil compaction and nutrient runoff during wet winter months. |
| Ireland[](https://t.co/NTYKTnTTyu) / Western UK | Optimal cow comfort; minimal heat stress | Heavy rainfall requires high drainage to prevent mud and foot rot. |
| Argentine Pampas[](https://t.co/slPSnOAVY4) | Large open tracts of flat grazing land | Summer temperatures occasionally require artificial or natural shade. |
| US Pacific Northwest Coast[](https://t.co/q2404pvgk4) | Moderate temperatures year-round | Summer dry spells require specific deep-rooting grasses. |

text:
The Black Hills, Gold, and a Broken Treaty

The Black Hills were never empty, and the Lakota were not the first people there.

Hunters used those dark pines at least 12,000 years ago. Clovis, Folsom, and later Archaic camps show up in the archaeological record. Rock art in the Hills goes back that far. We don’t have the names of those peoples. They hunted bison, worked stone, and moved with the seasons. For thousands of years the Hills were a hunting ground and a place of shelter, not a permanent homeland with fixed settlements or villages.

By the 1400s and 1500s, people from the Missouri were coming in. The Arikara, Pawnee kin who farmed along the river, hunted, cut timber, and traded in the Hills in summer, then went home to earth-lodge towns. Mandan and Hidatsa did the same. That pattern may have lasted for centuries. Smallpox on the Missouri in the late 1700s wrecked those villages and helped open the country west of the river.

In the 1700s the Hills themselves were Crow, Kiowa, and Kiowa-Apache ground, with Cheyenne and Arapaho moving in from the east. Bear Butte was already a Cheyenne holy place. People did not settle the timber in large villages. They came for lodge poles, game, medicine, and prayer, then returned to the open plains.

The Lakota came later, from the woodlands east of the Missouri. Horses and guns changed the math. An Oglala winter count puts a party under Standing Bull in the Hills around 1775. Over the next fifty years Lakota bands fought their way in. They pushed the Kiowa south onto the southern plains and drove the Crow west toward the Powder and Bighorn. First they fought the Cheyenne, then allied with them. By the early 1800s the Lakota were the power on the eastern side of the Hills. 

That is how Paha Sapa became Lakota country, not by a deed but by war and horses, the same way the plains were being remade everywhere.

They called the place Paha Sapa, known as “Wamaka Ognaka Ičante,” “the heart of everything that is.” Their camps stayed on the prairie. They entered the Hills for ceremony, timber, and burial. The buffalo remained on the grass. The hills kept the sacred work.

In 1868 the United States put a Lakota claim on paper. The Fort Laramie Treaty said the Black Hills were theirs, undisturbed. For a few years the promise held, mostly because the Army was tired and most Americans still thought the hills were only a rumor of dark trees.

Whites wanted the land for reasons that stacked up fast. Before anyone published a gold strike, there were already stories of minerals, thick timber, and grass around the edges that looked like farm and ranch country. After the Civil War the West was the outlet for restless men, railroads, and a government that wanted the plains settled and the tribes confined. The Panic of 1873 made hard money look like salvation. Gold was the spark that made the rest official.

Custer’s 1874 expedition was sold as a search for a fort site, but miners rode with the column. They panned color on French Creek. Newspapers treated it like a second California. Once that word hit the East, the treaty was finished. Washington could not, or would not, drag ten thousand prospectors back out. It was cheaper, politically, to break the paper than to enforce it.

What the miners wanted was placer gold in the creeks, then quartz veins in the rock. Deadwood, Custer City, and Lead rose out of mud and raw lumber. The Homestake strike turned a rush into an industry. Timber fed the mills and the towns. Cattlemen wanted the surrounding grass. The Army wanted posts and roads so the plains could be crossed without asking anyone. Speculators wanted town lots. The government wanted the tribes reduced to agencies and rations so the map would look finished.

Creeks that had run clear ran brown. Washington offered to buy the Hills. Sitting Bull picked up a pinch of dirt and said he would not sell even that much. Crazy Horse didn’t come to the talks. Money was the white measure. The Lakota answer was that the grandmother was not for sale.

In late 1875 the government set a deadline: report to the reservation by January 1876 or be called hostile. Winter is a bad month to move children and thin horses. Many bands were already out hunting because the agencies had little meat. The order was a war dressed as paperwork.

That summer Lakota and Cheyenne fighters won on the Rosebud and the Little Bighorn. The victory bought a season, not the land. The Army came back in the snow. In 1877 the Hills were taken under an agreement that never met the treaty’s own rule, consent of three-fourths of the men.
Gold paid. Towns stayed. 

The story is older than Custer and older than the Lakota. Gold, timber, grass, railroads, and a broken treaty turned the Hills from a promise into a prize. The pines still look black from a distance. Up close, they remember.

text:
I’ve been parsing government budgets and tracking how they actually handle their money since 1987 when I was in high school about 20 miles outside of DC. I started because I spent a lot of time with homeless Vietnam vets and I was being told that there was millions of dollars to help them but I couldn’t find a single agency or NPO that was actually providing services because they all claimed they didn’t have any money. And no one could explain where money on a line item clearly identified in the budget really was. 

Now, like you, I hate trotting out my bona fides but I started my first business when I was 19 and had to take a course on business accounting offered by my community college, I was an independent government contractor by 20, I had Fortune 100 multinational clients by 21, and I was in city government by 27. So, I know the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) more from a small business perspective and government accounting and spending because I was the person who authorized spending government money.  I’m not sure what’s going on there, but I can tell you that whatever you’ve found isn’t what you think it is because governments use this crazy budget process where they pass a budget for a fiscal year that includes spending in the future as if it’s being spent in the fiscal year, doesn’t include money they’re spending from previous fiscal years, misrepresents how they pay contractors or if there’s performance requirements to pay, and absolutely has line items for phantom expenses. 

California actually pays contractors in advance for work scheduled years in the future, the federal government is still paying on a contract that never met production deadlines for a project that was never feasible to a company that no longer exists, and my own state, Missouri, has declined to do legislatively required audits for certain agencies with some very illogical reasons. I’m going to assume that you know more about accounting than I do and simply ask: have you done a line-by-line study of the budgets going back at least 10 years?

Yes, a lot of fraud originates in pandemic spending but if you do an historical analysis you’ll probably find that the amount of money written by checks doesn’t equate to anything in the budget because they’re paying with current funds what they claim they already paid based on previous budgets and they’re paying today for projects that don’t start for years. 

It’s the craziest method of accounting I’ve ever seen and it’s getting harder to parse out where the actual checks are going because they just lump things together in the budget and then never put out the reconciliation of their accounts.

Judge: “Your financial circumstances would improve substantially if you took this job?”

Mother: “Yes.”

Judge: “But the children would lose regular in-person contact with an actively involved parent.”

Mother: “We’d replace it with longer visits.”

Judge: “You can’t replace a Wednesday night dinner with a FaceTime call.”

The mother looked down.

Judge: “The court is not deciding whether California offers you a better opportunity.”

He looked at both parents.

Judge: “It’s deciding whether relocating these children is in their best interests.”

He picked up the order.

Ethiopian elites have repeatedly acted on a sense of «entitlement» only to discover later that what looked like a brilliant strategic move was, in fact, a spectacular mistake. 

Today, Abiy Ahmed and his supporters are once again entertaining the fantasy of turning landlocked Ethiopia into a Red Sea maritime state through "militarily" by invading the Eritrean coastal territory such as Assab. 😆 

If that gamble ever turns into a disaster with some unintended long-term strategic consequences, don’t be surprised when the same people eventually look back and say the same familiar words: “It was a mistake.”

The problem is that history doesn’t offer a rewind button. By the time the reality they never anticipated arrives, saying “we made a mistake” may be the easiest part.

Why India’s Port Giants Are the Ultimate "Tollbooths" of a $4 Trillion Economy?

If you want to play India’s manufacturing explosion, don’t just look at factories, look at the gateways. Over 95% of India’s trade volume moves by sea, making port infrastructure the ultimate tollbooth for the nation’s $1 trillion export ambition. With mega-policy pushes like PM Gati Shakti, the Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2030 and global trade shifts under China+1, India's coastlines are rapidly morphing into high-speed logistics highways. Port operators aren't just cyclical transport plays; they are long-term, high-margin gatekeepers of a booming $4 trillion economy.

Enter the private duopoly of scale: Adani Ports & Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) and JSW Infrastructure. These companies enjoy ironclad economic moats that are virtually impossible to replicate - astronomical entry barriers, 30 to 50 year concessions and prime coastal real estate. APSEZ stands as the undisputed titan, controlling a coast-to-coast network that handles over a third of India's commercial cargo. Meanwhile, JSW Infrastructure is executing a high-octane growth playbook, backed by built-in "anchor cargo" from its parent conglomerate while aggressively expanding its capacity toward 400 MTPA by 2030.

The real kicker? They are evolving from simple port operators into end-to-end supply chain powerhouses. By integrating deep-water ports with dedicated freight rail networks, inland container depots, and multi-modal logistics, APSEZ and JSW Infra lock in sticky, long-term customer contracts with immense pricing power. As containerization rates rise and trade volumes compound faster than national GDP growth, these port giants offer predictable, inflation-protected cash flows - making them one of the most compelling long-term compounders of India’s decade-long infrastructure boom.

text:
Does the wind at the Bali United Training Center interfere with training?🌬️

Its strategic location on the shores of Purnama Beach offers stunning views, but also offers a unique natural feature: the sea breeze. Several coaches who have taken their teams to training there, including when Pohang Steelers used the facility, have mentioned that the wind can be strong and requires adjustment.

Wind blowing from the sea can affect the direction of the ball, especially during technical training or set-pieces. However, until now, this has been considered more of a natural challenge than a serious disruption. Players and coaches generally adjust training sessions based on weather conditions, similar to what happens at many coastal training grounds around the world.

So, do balls often "run" into the sea? With a safety zone of approximately 10 meters around the field and the field's location not directly on the edge of the surf, the possibility of balls going into the sea is certainly present, but it's not a significant problem that disrupts daily training. The staff and players are undoubtedly familiar with this situation.

The combination of a FIFA-standard pitch surrounded by the sea is what makes the Bali United Training Center unique and highly acclaimed. The wind and proximity to the sea are elements of the location's character, not a drawback. 

What do you think? Is the sea breeze at the Training Center more of a challenge or an attraction? Leave your comments below.👇

🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 America is bombing Iran again tonight... just hours after Iran rejected the Gulf's plan to share the Strait of Hormuz

The retaliation came right on schedule. 

CENTCOM announced strikes on Iran tonight in answer to the missile attack on the Jordan base, and Iranian media reported explosions rolling across the south, Bandar Abbas, Bushehr, Qeshm, the same coastal map America has hit for months. 

Larry Johnson, thirty years across CIA and State, calls it Groundhog Day: hitting a ball of mercury with a hammer, scattering the problem instead of destroying it.

The bigger story broke hours earlier at the negotiating table. 

Oman, backed by the Gulf states, formally offered Iran a 50/50 joint management plan for the strait with voluntary contributions modeled on the Strait of Malacca. 

Iran rejected it as unreasonable, and Reuters revealed what Tehran actually wants: sole control over everything sailing in, shared control over what sails out. 

Washington's response was just as absolute, no tolls and no fees, EVER.

Larry's decode is that nobody should be surprised, since the original MOU named exactly one country responsible for passage through the strait, and Iran has simply never left that position.

So both doors closed on the same day, and the military door leads nowhere better.

The remaining Patriot interceptors split across three theaters leave roughly 140 shots for this one by his math, and the new plan for two more weeks of heavy strikes repeats the exact plan that already failed. 

"This is Einstein's definition of insanity, doing the same thing over and over and expecting a different outcome."

Bombs by night, rejections by day.

The war has found its rhythm, and neither side is dancing toward the exit.

text:
A US court ruled the First Amendment protects possession of AI-generated child rape media, “no real child appears in them.” This makes it harder for investigators who are already struggling with child rapists distorting real images to look like AI. #OpDeathEaters
--------------------------------------------------------

A federal appeals court struck down the US ban on possessing AI-generated child rape media inside the home on 25 August, holding that the First Amendment protects such material where it depicts no real child.
The Seventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal of one count against Steven Anderegg, 42, of Holmen, Wisconsin, whose prosecution the Justice Department brought in May 2024 as its first federal case over child rape media generated entirely by artificial intelligence.
Judge John Lee, writing for a panel that also included Doris Pryor and Joshua Kolar, held the possession provision of 18 U.S.C. § 1466A unconstitutional as applied to Anderegg across 27 pages. Lee, joined by Kolar, filed a separate concurrence asking the Supreme Court to revisit the 2002 decision that controls the question.

Section 1466A(b)(1) is the provision that reaches a person who obtains obscene synthetic child rape media without producing it or passing it on. Prosecutors in the circuit covering Wisconsin, Illinois and Indiana no longer have that count available where the images depict no identifiable child and stay inside the defendant's home.

How the case began
Meta reported an Instagram direct message to the CyberTipline run by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children in October 2023, after Anderegg sent sexually explicit AI-generated images to an account belonging to a 15-year-old boy and told the boy in the same exchange how he had produced it.

Investigators executing a search warrant found Stable Diffusion installed on Anderegg's laptop, modified with add-on components that gave the model the ability to render human genitalia. The Justice Department put the total haul at roughly 13,000 images. Hundreds of them showed nude or semi-clothed prepubescent minors displaying or touching their genitals, alongside the curated text prompts and the negative prompts Anderegg used to keep adult bodies out of the output.

A grand jury indicted him on 15 May 2024 on four counts under § 1466A: production, distribution, transfer of obscene material to a minor under 16 and possession. Prosecutors put his maximum exposure at 70 years with a five-year mandatory minimum, and he was detained pending a hearing on 22 May 2024.

"CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM, and we will hold accountable those who exploit AI to create obscene, abusive, and increasingly photorealistic images of children," then-Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco said when the charges were announced.

The government conceded during the litigation that the images depicted no actual child and could not be traced to one. The concession took Ferber and Osborne out of the case and left Stanley and Free Speech Coalition to decide it.

Chief Judge James Peterson of the Western District of Wisconsin dismissed the possession count on 13 February 2025 and left the other three standing. Prosecutors took an interlocutory appeal. William Clayman and Ross Goldman of the Justice Department's criminal division argued it on 30 October 2025 against Joseph Bugni of Hurley Burish, who represents Anderegg. The panel took just under 10 months to rule.

A statute written for the last technology
Congress passed § 1466A in 2003 as part of the PROTECT Act, drafted in direct response to the Supreme Court striking down the Child Pornography Prevention Act the year before. Subsection (c) states that it is not a required element that the minor depicted actually exist. Subsection (f)(1) reaches any "digital image or picture, computer image or picture, or computer generated image".

Obscenity is the ingredient Congress added to keep the statute inside the constitutional line, and § 1466A(b)(1) bites only where the material meets that standard. Lee assumed for the sake of argument that Anderegg's images did, then held the statute still could not reach them in his house.

Two precedents, four rejected arguments
Stanley v. Georgia, decided in 1969, bars prosecution for private possession of obscene material at home, on the reasoning that government has "no business telling a man, sitting alone in his own house" what books he may read or what films he may watch. Lee wrote that the holding "was predicated on the location, the home", rather than on the character of what was found there.

Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition, decided in 2002, struck down federal bans on computer-generated abuse imagery involving no real child. New York v. Ferber and Osborne v. Ohio, which place abuse imagery of real children outside First Amendment protection altogether, rest on the permanent record of an actual child's abuse and the economic motive that distribution supplies to producers. No real child appears in Anderegg's files, so the panel held that neither case reaches his conduct.

Prosecutors offered four reasons to override Stanley, and Lee traced each one to a passage in Free Speech Coalition rejecting it. On the government's case that offenders use such imagery to groom children, Lee quoted the Supreme Court's answer that government "may not prohibit speech because it increases the chance an unlawful act will be committed at some indefinite future time".

 On the case that synthetic material normalises abuse, the Supreme Court had demanded a significantly stronger and more direct connection to actual harm. On the case that virtual images substitute for the real market, the Supreme Court had called the theory implausible, since producers would switch to fictional images and escape prosecution altogether. On the case that AI output has become impossible to tell from photographs of real abuse, straining investigators, the Supreme Court had written that government "may not suppress lawful speech as the means to suppress unlawful speech".

Prosecutors also told the court that § 1466A(b)(1) survives because it reaches only material shipped or transported in interstate commerce, an element Stanley's statute lacked. Lee rejected the distinction on the ground that the eight-millimetre reels seized from Stanley's desk drawer had almost certainly crossed state lines as well, and treated the commerce element as jurisdictional rather than a description of anything wrongful.

A footnote set out federal sentencing data showing that nearly 44 per cent of possession offenders had engaged in aggravating conduct, alongside a caveat that the social science on whether viewing such imagery causes contact offending remains inconclusive. Another footnote flagged morphed images, which paste a real child's face onto another body, as sitting closer to Ferber. The panel did not decide that question.

Counts one through three remain live, and the opinion leaves untouched any prosecution for producing or sharing the same files.

The concurrence
Lee wrote separately, joined by Kolar, that the court would "benefit from additional guidance from the Supreme Court regarding the intersection between the First Amendment and virtual CSAM", and that in the years since Free Speech Coalition the technology has reached a point where AI output is virtually indistinguishable from images of physical abuse. Only in recent months, the concurrence said, have the tools become good enough to fool the human eye.
Justice Clarence Thomas anticipated the problem in 2002. Concurring in the judgment in Free Speech Coalition, he wrote that "if technological advances thwart prosecution of 'unlawful speech,' the Government may well have a compelling interest in barring or otherwise regulating some narrow category of 'lawful speech'". Justice Sandra Day O'Connor would have upheld the ban on virtual imagery indistinguishable from the real thing.

Lee cited testimony that the influx of synthetic material imposes growing burdens on investigators and lets offenders disguise pictures of real children by making the images look computer-generated, which slows the identification of actual victims among the files police recover.

Researchers at the Stanford Internet Observatory, led by chief technologist David Thiel, reported on 20 December 2023 that LAION-5B, the open dataset behind Stable Diffusion, contained 3,226 suspected instances of child sexual abuse material, of which 1,008 were externally validated. LAION withdrew the dataset and published a cleaned version, Re-LAION-5B, in August 2024. Demand for AI-generated material can therefore raise demand for the real abuse imagery the models train on, Lee wrote, which is the harm Osborne was decided to prevent.

21 million reports
NCMEC received 21.3 million CyberTipline reports in 2025. More than 400,000 of them carried what the organisation calls a generative AI nexus, and more than 182,000 involved offenders possessing, generating or attempting to generate AI abuse material. NCMEC has categorised 158,000 images and videos as AI-generated abuse material since 2023 and identified more than 275 victims of it.

Riana Pfefferkorn of Stanford, who predicted before the indictment that prosecutors would fall back on obscenity statutes for AI cases, wrote to NCMEC on 29 January 2026 to flag what those totals conceal. A Bloomberg investigation had found Amazon's 380,000 reports flagged as AI-related contained no AI-generated material at all, but known abuse imagery surfaced while scanning training data. 

Nearly 80 per cent of all generative AI CyberTipline reports in the first half of 2025 involved no AI-generated abuse material, Pfefferkorn wrote, and the single checkbox that produced the figure had misled lawmakers and researchers for six months. NCMEC itself notes that more than 10 per cent of industry reports arrive with inadequate information.

The Internet Watch Foundation logged 3,443 AI-generated abuse videos in 2025, against 13 the year before, a count drawn from material its analysts assessed directly rather than from industry self-reporting.

The law elsewhere
State legislatures moved faster than the federal courts. As of August 2026, 46 US states criminalise AI-generated or computer-edited abuse material, more than half of those laws passed in 2024 and 2025, according to the tracker maintained by Enough Abuse. Colorado, Massachusetts, Ohio, Vermont and the District of Columbia have no such statute. Oklahoma, Utah, Arkansas and Florida reach wholly fictional depictions; most of the rest require an identifiable minor or the manipulation of a real image, which leaves them closer to the morphed-image question the Seventh Circuit declined to answer.
Section 163.1 of Canada's Criminal Code reaches depictions of imaginary children. The Supreme Court of Canada held in R v Sharpe in 2001 that "person" in the definition covers both actual and imaginary human beings, and upheld the possession offence subject to narrow carve-outs for private material a person creates and keeps for himself alone.

England and Wales criminalise pseudo-photographs under the Protection of Children Act 1978 and non-photographic prohibited images under section 62 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009. The Crime and Policing Act 2026, which received royal assent on 29 April 2026, created an offence of adapting, possessing, supplying or offering to supply a child sexual abuse image generator, carrying five years. The same Act extended section 69 of the Serious Crime Act 2015, on paedophile manuals, to cover pseudo-photographs and prohibited images.

How the ruling was reported
The Federalist ran the headline "Judge: Child Sex Abuse Images Are OK If They're Made With AI" on 28 August, one of several treatments casting the ruling as a judge legalising synthetic child rape media. The decision reaches in-home possession alone, leaves production, distribution and transfer to a minor fully prosecutable and rests on Supreme Court precedent the panel said it had no authority to set aside. "We are not free to redraw them ourselves", Lee wrote of the lines the Supreme Court has drawn, adding that the court leaves to the Supreme Court the prerogative of overruling its own decisions.

Hans von Spakovsky of Advancing American Freedom said that "AI-generated images are now virtually indistinguishable from the real thing and some of these images may be created based on real child sexual abuse material".

The Justice Department can seek rehearing before the full Seventh Circuit or petition the Supreme Court, which under its Rule 13 allows 90 days from the entry of judgment to file for certiorari, putting the date at 23 November 2026 unless a rehearing petition resets the clock. No decision has been announced.

Anderegg still faces trial in the Western District of Wisconsin on the three surviving counts.

Where the ruling can still be challenged
The Office of the Solicitor General decides whether the United States petitions the Supreme Court, and it has announced nothing. Rule 13 allows 90 days from the entry of judgment, putting the date at 23 November 2026, and a timely petition for rehearing before the full Seventh Circuit would restart the clock from its denial. Both moves are discretionary calls inside the Justice Department that lost the appeal, and neither carries a public comment process.
S.3021, the ENFORCE Act, passed the Senate by unanimous consent on 16 December 2025 and was held at the House desk the following day, where it has sat for eight months without a scheduled vote. John Cornyn sponsored it with Richard Blumenthal, John Kennedy and Mike Lee. Constituents pressing for a floor vote have one named target each, their own House member.

The bill strips the statute of limitations from obscene depictions of child sexual abuse, requires sex offender registration, presumes pre-trial detention, mandates supervised release and tightens the knowledge element on interstate transport. None of that restores a possession charge for images depicting no real child. The obstacle in Anderegg is Stanley, not the drafting of § 1466A, and Congress cannot amend a Supreme Court precedent.

Colorado, Massachusetts, Ohio, Vermont and the District of Columbia have no statute reaching AI-generated or computer-edited abuse material, which leaves a live bill to write for residents of those five jurisdictions. Stanley was itself a Georgia prosecution, so a new state ban on possession inside the home meets the same barrier the Seventh Circuit applied. State law reaching production, distribution and possession outside the home is untouched by the ruling.

Nothing in US federal law matches the offence England and Wales created on 29 April 2026 of adapting, possessing, supplying or offering to supply a child sexual abuse image generator, carrying five years. An offence aimed at the tool rather than at the file in a person's house falls outside what Stanley covers, and no bill before Congress creates one.
LAION withdrew its dataset and published a cleaned version after the Stanford finding, on its own initiative. No US statute requires a model developer to audit training data for abuse material or to disclose what an audit found.

NCMEC's reporting form carries a single generative AI checkbox, which produced the 80 per cent miscount Pfefferkorn identified, and she has asked the organisation to replace it with granular options. Congress, the courts and the concurrence in this case all cite figures drawn from that form.

Overturning the holding itself takes the Supreme Court revisiting Free Speech Coalition and narrowing Stanley, which is what Lee and Kolar asked for in writing, or an amendment to the Constitution. No lower court in the Seventh Circuit can reach it

📊 REIT Earnings Quick Takes

Broadstone Net Lease (BNL) - a diversified net lease REIT that has increasingly emphasized build-to-suit development as a higher-return alternative to highly competitive conventional acquisitions - traded lower by 3% today despite reporting an in-line quarter while raising its 2026 earnings and investment outlook.

Second-quarter AFFO of $0.39/share increased 2.6% year-over-year and matched consensus. BNL raised its full-year AFFO range to $1.55-$1.57/share from $1.53-$1.57, lifting the midpoint by $0.01 to $1.56 and implying roughly 4% annual growth. 

The increase reflects stronger investment assumptions and lower expected bad debt, with full-year investment guidance raised to $600M -$800M from $500M -$625M and the credit-loss assumption reduced to 50 basis points from 75 basis points.

Portfolio fundamentals remained stable, with same-store rental revenue increasing 2.2%, supported by contractual rent escalators and prior leasing activity. BNL ended the quarter at effectively 100% occupancy, collected 99.9% of base rent, and increased investment-grade tenant exposure by 100 basis points to 20.1% of annual rent. 

Industrial properties generated 3.3% same-store growth, while weaker performance across other property types moderated the consolidated result.

The key story remains BNL’s rapidly expanding build-to-suit platform, which now includes 12 committed or in-process projects totaling approximately $645M at expected initial cash yields of 7.9% and straight-line yields of 9.9%. 

Subsequent to quarter-end, BNL commenced a $303M advanced-technology facility in Colorado for a Fortune 20 investment-grade tenant under a 15-year triple-net lease with 3% annual rent increases. Rent commencement is expected by March 2027, with a projected straight-line yield of approximately 11.6%.

On the call, BNL noted that build-to-suit opportunities currently offer more attractive risk-adjusted returns than regular-way acquisitions, including targeted levered returns above 20%. The principal constraint remains leverage, which ended the quarter relatively elevated compared to its peers at 6.4x, although $1B of liquidity and $163M of unsettled forward equity provide capacity to fund the development pipeline.

@POTUS @realDonaldTrump This is who you endorsed!

Mike Lindell (commonly misspelled “Lindel”), the MyPillow CEO, is not generally considered trustworthy on the high-profile claims that define his public profile, particularly 2020 election fraud allegations. Assessments depend on context, but his record shows repeated promotion of claims that courts, arbitrators, fact-checkers, and election officials have rejected as baseless or false. 

Lindell founded MyPillow and became widely known through infomercials. He has a personal recovery story involving overcoming a severe cocaine addiction through religious conversion, which he discusses openly. His company has sold large volumes of pillows, but it has faced criticism for advertising practices. The Better Business Bureau revoked its accreditation and lowered its rating to an F, citing a pattern of complaints and a continuous “buy one, get one free” offer that effectively became the regular price rather than a limited promotion. 

His most significant controversies involve post-2020 election claims. Lindell has asserted that Dominion and Smartmatic voting systems, foreign interference (including China), and specific individuals (such as former Dominion executive Eric Coomer) helped steal the election from Donald Trump. These claims have been rejected in multiple venues:A Colorado jury found him and related entities liable for defaming Coomer, ordering roughly $2.3 million in damages; a judge later declined to overturn the verdict. 

A federal judge ruled that Lindell made false statements defaming Smartmatic; issues of actual malice and damages remained for further proceedings, and he has faced contempt findings related to discovery. 

Dominion sued him and MyPillow for $1.3 billion over similar claims; the suit ended in a confidential settlement (the company, later rebranded, dismissed the case). 

In his own “Prove Mike Wrong” challenge offering $5 million, an arbitrator initially ruled that software expert Robert Zeidman had shown the provided data was not related to the election and was entitled to the prize (Lindell later won an appeal on procedural/contract interpretation grounds). 

Courts, state and federal officials, and independent reviews found no credible evidence supporting the scale of fraud Lindell described. He has continued promoting the claims despite adverse rulings and financial strain from the legal battles. Retailers dropped or reduced MyPillow products amid the controversies (Lindell attributed this to politics; some cited demand).Trustworthiness is not binary and can vary by domain. Product quality reviews for MyPillow are mixed, as with many consumer goods. Lindell’s personal recovery narrative is his own account and has been part of his branding. However, on election integrity—the area where he has been most vocal and influential as a Trump ally and political activist—his major public assertions have not withstood legal or evidentiary scrutiny. He is currently a 2026 Minnesota gubernatorial candidate with Trump’s endorsement and continues facing legal and financial pressures tied to these matters. In short, reliance on his statements about 2020 election processes or related conspiracy claims is not supported by the available record of court outcomes and investigations. text:
This video, created by Kenganda, serves as a critical commentary on recent statements made by Professor James Small regarding Black identity, Pan-Africanism, and the Foundational Black American (FBA) movement.  The host, Oshay Duke Jackson, analyzes Professor Small's arguments and offers a counter-perspective on the current state of these ideological discussions.

Key themes and analysis:

Identity and Categorization: Professor Small asserts that 'Africa is a race' and 'America is a place,' arguing that rejecting the label 'African' constitutes a lack of commitment to fighting white supremacy or is a form of self-hatred. Jackson criticizes this as an emotional argument and 'gaslighting,' suggesting that for many, these labels are about finding a functional, mutually beneficial identity rather than denying history.

Disparity in Expectations: Jackson points out a double standard where Professor Small seemingly allows other groups to use hyphenated identities (e.g., Jamaican-American) but restricts Black Americans to a specific, singular definition of 'African'.

The Need for Value Exchange: The video argues that movements like Pan-Africanism fail to gain traction when there is no tangible, equitable 'value exchange' between parties. It compares the tension in these ideological spaces to local geopolitical struggles in Africa, emphasizing that collaboration requires fairness.

Criticism of 'Chameleon' Rhetoric: Jackson highlights past instances where Professor Small has criticized Africans for being disconnected from the struggles of Black Americans, accusing him of shifting his narrative depending on the context.

Conclusion: Jackson ultimately labels Professor Small's recent remarks as an intellectual failure and 'outdated,' despite acknowledging him as a brilliant historian. He concludes that for Pan-Africanism to remain relevant, it must move beyond shaming language and address the actual, day-to-day needs of the community.

text:
The Breakfast Queen’s Long Shadow
Or: How the Indomitable Interrogator Became a Masterclass in Selective Outrage

There is a certain type of broadcaster who thrives on the romance of the tough working-class outsider.

Kay Burley has long been its most polished practitioner. The Wigan girl made good. The fearless breakfast interrogator who “set the agenda.” The woman who, we were assured, asked the questions others were too polite to pose, who made politicians of every stripe squirm, and who somehow remained the authentic voice of robust, independent journalism even as the complaints mounted and the suspensions arrived.

Even her presentation has been carefully curated into something almost heroic — the indomitable northern warrior, all grit and no nonsense, as if decades of selective fire and personal exemption could be smoothed away with the right backstory.

One is invited to examine the record before swallowing the legend.

As the long-serving face of Sky News breakfast, Ms Burley made the robust questioning of Conservative ministers a personal speciality. The interruptions were sharp. The moral tone was elevated. The public were repeatedly invited to share her indignation at rule-breaking, at “one rule for us and one rule for them.”

Then came December 2020.

At the height of the tiered restrictions she had spent months policing from the studio, she celebrated her sixtieth birthday with a multi-household gathering that breached the very rules she had so energetically enforced upon others.

Restaurant-hopping. Curfew-breaking. Colleagues present.

The subsequent six-month suspension was presented, with characteristic understatement, as an inadvertent slip — a brief need for the facilities. The earlier lectures to ministers and the public were left unexamined.

One does not need to exaggerate. The gap between the rhetoric of accountability and the lived practice was noticeable enough.

The broader pattern of aggression is no less instructive. 

Over the years the same style produced a remarkable catalogue: the interview that reduced Peter Andre to tears; the Alton Towers chief executive subjected to such sustained hostility that petitions for her removal gathered tens of thousands of signatures; the search volunteers for a missing child informed, live on air, that police expected the worst; the photographer reportedly seized by the throat outside court; the CAGE interviewee told to “get over yourself” after walking out. 

Ofcom files grew thick. The defence was always the same: robust journalism.

Yet the direction of travel was rarely even-handed. 

Election nights and morning slots tended to reveal a particular appetite for Conservative discomfort.

The laughter that accompanied the 2024 Labour landslide graphic was noted at the time. Recent social-media activity continues the habit: pointed reminders to former Conservative home secretaries of boat numbers under their watch, sharp replies to former prime ministers. The energy that once made Tory ministers flinch has not been retired with the Sky contract.

Even the more recent interventions carry the same imprint.

On Newsnight this month, seated beside an Epstein survivor who had just urged other victims to come forward, Ms Burley interjected that the former Duke of York should be accepted as a “war hero.”

The studio reaction was instructive. One hundred and sixty complaints followed. The phrase was offered with the same brisk confidence that once characterised her lockdown lectures.

Having left the breakfast chair, she remains active — still framing questions, still allocating moral weight, still inviting the audience to share her particular sense of outrage. The method is continuous: popular indignation first, consistency later.

This is the classic sequence of media performance politics. A public figure spends years demanding standards while the music plays. When the music stops, the exemption is revealed and the arithmetic of reputation becomes awkward.

The British public is being invited to believe that the woman who could not apply to herself the rules she so vigorously policed for others remains the gold standard of fearless interrogation. It is a generous invitation.

History suggests it should be received with rather more caution than enthusiasm.

The studio lights are still on. One rather wonders who will still be nodding when they finally go out.

Yours in watchful scepticism,
A Gentleman from the Old School
