text:
$PWR KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM QUANTA SERVICES Q2 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Quanta Services’ Q2 2026 call provides unusually strong confirmation that the North American power-infrastructure cycle is broadening from conventional utility transmission and distribution into generation, data-center power systems, mechanical and electrical construction, advanced manufacturing, modular fabrication, renewables and natural-gas infrastructure. The quality of the signal is high because the acquisitions completed during the quarter contributed only approximately $11 million of adjusted EBITDA, management identified no material revenue pull-forward or unusual project-closeout benefit, and the company nevertheless reported $9.6 billion of revenue, $1.1 billion of adjusted EBITDA, $4.24 of adjusted EPS, robust free cash flow and record backlog of approximately $53 billion. The most consequential cross-market conclusions are that gas-generation capacity will remain scarce for years, the large-transmission cycle has not yet entered the field at scale, high-voltage equipment and skilled craft labor remain structural bottlenecks, data-center infrastructure demand is converting faster than reported backlog captures, and Quanta’s integrated self-perform model is increasingly capable of taking scope from fragmented contractors. The principal negative read-throughs are higher capital intensity and energization risk for hyperscalers and utilities, potential relative share pressure on stand-alone engineering and construction providers, and evidence that commercial deployment of 800-volt data-center architecture remains behind the most aggressive market expectations.

POWER GENERATION AND MERCHANT POWER

GAS-TURBINE SCARCITY EXTENDS THE VALUE OF BOTH OEM CAPACITY AND EXISTING GENERATION (READ-THROUGH 1)

Call evidence: Management identified generation and generation EPC capacity as among the most important bottlenecks in the power market. Duke Austin stated that “if you order an engine today, you’re 5 years out, probably 6 before you get them built.” Quanta is seeing demand for both front-of-meter and behind-the-meter generation, including small and large engines, but is unwilling to accept conventional combined-cycle or single-cycle EPC risk unless customers provide appropriate contractual protections. Management also specifically indicated confidence that GE Vernova’s generation bookings would remain strong.

Affected companies and impact: GE Vernova (GEV: US) — Positive, high magnitude; Siemens Energy (ENR: Germany) — Positive, high magnitude; Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (7011: Japan) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude; Vistra (VST: US) — Positive, high magnitude; Talen Energy (TLN: US) — Positive, high magnitude; Constellation Energy (CEG: US) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude; NRG Energy (NRG: US) — Positive, moderate magnitude. Amazon (AMZN: US), Microsoft (MSFT: US), Alphabet (GOOGL: US) and Meta Platforms (META: US) face a negative, moderate-magnitude near-term read-through through higher power-procurement costs, longer energization timelines and increased reliance on interim generation solutions.

The positive OEM transmission mechanism is straightforward. Lead times extending to approximately 5-6 years indicate that demand materially exceeds immediately available manufacturing and EPC capacity. This supports elevated order intake, larger customer deposits, improved contractual protections, pricing power and longer revenue visibility for the limited number of large-frame gas-turbine suppliers. The signal is particularly valuable because it comes from an infrastructure contractor engaged with utilities and large-load customers at the project-development stage, rather than solely from turbine manufacturers reporting their own order books.

The less obvious but equally important read-through is positive for owners of existing dispatchable generation. If new gas plants cannot be ordered, engineered, permitted and constructed quickly enough to meet accelerating electricity demand, the scarcity value of operating nuclear, gas and selected coal assets persists for longer. Vistra and Talen have particularly direct exposure to constrained merchant-power regions, while Constellation benefits from the increasing strategic and economic value of an operating nuclear fleet. Delayed newbuild capacity can support higher capacity prices, stronger bilateral contracting economics and improved terminal values for existing plants.

The near-term trading catalysts are further turbine order announcements, increasing customer deposits, additional long-term power contracts and evidence that utilities or hyperscalers are paying premiums for accelerated equipment slots. The longer-duration fundamental shift is that supply scarcity may persist into the early 2030s even if turbine manufacturers increase capacity, because manufacturing expansion does not eliminate permitting, engineering, construction-labor and interconnection constraints.

The negative consequence is concentrated among new-load developers and utilities. Behind-the-meter generation can accelerate initial energization, but it is not a frictionless substitute for utility-scale supply. Customers must absorb higher equipment costs, fuel-delivery requirements, emissions permitting, operating complexity and potentially lower efficiency. The call therefore supports the earnings durability of existing generation and OEM suppliers, but it simultaneously raises the capital required to translate AI and industrial-load demand into operating computing or manufacturing capacity.

GRID TRANSMISSION AND REGULATED UTILITIES

THE LARGE-TRANSMISSION AND GENERATION CONSTRUCTION CYCLE HAS NOT YET ENTERED REPORTED RESULTS AT SCALE (READ-THROUGH 2)

Call evidence: Management stated that the traditional transmission and distribution business is already capable of approximately upper-single-digit to double-digit growth before the largest programs begin. Approximately 95% of the larger generation work was described as not yet included in backlog. Major 765-kV, 500-kV and 345-kV programs remain in engineering, limited-notice-to-proceed or verbal-award stages. Management expects more of this work to enter backlog during 2H26, with meaningful field activity beginning in 2H27 and extending beyond 2030. Quanta explicitly referenced its collaborative 765-kV work with American Electric Power and indicated that a significant portion of the NiSource generation opportunity should enter backlog in Q3 2026.

Affected companies and impact: Quanta Services (PWR: US) — Positive, high magnitude; MYR Group (MYRG: US) — Positive, high magnitude; MasTec (MTZ: US) — Positive, moderate magnitude; Primoris Services (PRIM: US) — Positive, moderate magnitude; American Electric Power (AEP: US) — Positive long-term, moderate-to-high magnitude, but mixed near-term; NiSource (NI: US) — Positive long-term, moderate-to-high magnitude, but mixed near-term.

The most important implication is that current contractor revenues and backlogs do not yet represent the full transmission super-cycle. Quanta’s record backlog has been achieved while much of the largest incremental work remains in engineering or preconstruction. This creates a sequential earnings architecture: current base T&D growth supports 2026, large awards increase backlog during late 2026 and 2027, and field mobilization becomes a more substantial revenue and margin contributor from 2H27 onward. The cycle is therefore more likely to stack onto the current earnings base than to replace a fading near-term project cycle.

The read-through is strongest for Quanta and MYR Group because both have substantial exposure to high-voltage electric infrastructure and skilled electrical labor. MasTec and Primoris should benefit from higher utility investment, although the magnitude depends on project mix, customer relationships and their ability to secure labor without accepting disproportionate fixed-price risk. Quanta’s scale, training system and integrated service offering make it the clearest beneficiary, but the call validates the underlying demand environment for the broader contractor universe.

For American Electric Power and NiSource, the direction is fundamentally positive but financially more nuanced. Larger transmission and generation programs expand regulated asset bases and can support multi-year earnings growth if authorized returns, cost recovery and customer demand remain favorable. The near-term offset is greater capital intensity, financing requirements, regulatory scrutiny and ratepayer-affordability risk. A utility can therefore experience stronger long-term earnings growth while simultaneously facing pressure on free cash flow, credit metrics and equity issuance requirements.

The near-term trading catalyst is the conversion of engineering-stage projects into announced awards, RPO and backlog during Q3 and Q4 2026. The longer-duration shift begins when projects reach the field in 2H27 and labor utilization increases across multiple programs simultaneously. Quanta indicated that this stacking effect can produce higher margins through better utilization, but it will also create lumpier quarterly bookings because individual projects are large.

The principal negative risk is timing rather than demand. Permitting, rights-of-way, regulatory approvals, equipment availability and customer financing can delay project starts without eliminating the underlying requirement. Backlog and book-to-bill should consequently be evaluated across multiple quarters rather than treated as linear quarterly indicators.

ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT AND GRID COMPONENTS

CRITICAL HIGH-VOLTAGE EQUIPMENT REMAINS A SELLER’S MARKET (READ-THROUGH 3)

Call evidence: Management described high-voltage breakers as difficult to obtain and referenced Quanta’s breaker arrangement with privately held HICO. Quanta has also invested in transformer and utility-pole capabilities and stated that it will deploy capital wherever a component represents a critical path to project execution. Management’s broader message was that underinvestment in the vertical supply chain continues to constrain construction schedules.

Affected companies and impact: Eaton (ETN: US) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude; Hubbell (HUBB: US) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude; Powell Industries (POWL: US) — Positive, high magnitude relative to company size; GE Vernova (GEV: US) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude; Hitachi (6501: Japan), through Hitachi Energy — Positive, moderate magnitude. Utilities and hyperscalers are negatively affected at a moderate magnitude through higher equipment prices, earlier procurement commitments and greater working-capital requirements.

The most important read-through is that electrical-equipment tightness is not limited to a single product category. Breakers, transformers, poles, substations and associated high-voltage systems are all potential schedule-critical components. This supports a prolonged environment of strong order books, customer deposits, favorable price realization and extended visibility for manufacturers with qualified capacity.

Powell Industries has particularly high earnings sensitivity because data-center, utility and industrial electrical projects can materially affect a smaller revenue base. Eaton and Hubbell are more diversified, but the duration and breadth of grid investment support continued above-normal demand. GE Vernova and Hitachi Energy benefit from higher-voltage transmission and substation activity, in addition to their broader generation and grid portfolios.

Quanta’s willingness to invest directly in the supply chain is itself an important confirmation of scarcity. Contractors ordinarily prefer capital-light procurement when external supply is reliable. Vertical investment becomes rational when the economic value of schedule certainty exceeds the cost of owning or partnering for manufacturing capacity. This indicates that equipment availability can determine project timing and contractor revenue recognition, not merely component pricing.

The near-term catalyst is continued backlog expansion and pricing strength at equipment manufacturers. Customers may place orders earlier than historical norms to reserve capacity, supporting order books before field construction begins. The longer-term shift is greater integration between engineering, fabrication, equipment procurement and construction. Contractors that control more of the supply chain can reduce schedule risk and capture a larger portion of project economics.

The negative read-through is that selective contractor insourcing could eventually reduce third-party share in narrow product categories. However, the call suggests that aggregate demand is growing faster than available capacity, making the sector-level effect positive despite some risk of vertical integration. The public companies listed were not identified as direct Quanta suppliers on the call; the implication is based on their exposure to the constrained high-voltage equipment categories that management discussed.

DATA CENTERS AND LARGE-LOAD INFRASTRUCTURE

DATA-CENTER POWER-INFRASTRUCTURE DEMAND IS STRONGER THAN REPORTED BACKLOG ALONE SUGGESTS (READ-THROUGH 4)

Call evidence: Technology-related activity has grown to approximately 15%-20% of Quanta’s business in roughly 2 years, although management emphasized that this category includes semiconductors, manufacturing and other large-load facilities in addition to data centers. Quanta is increasingly contracting directly with hyperscalers and larger technology customers. Management stated that Quanta can address approximately 80%-90% of a data-center build excluding the computing chips and can “book and build $300 million on a site in a quarter” without the full activity becoming visible in reported backlog. Management also described data-center areas as 8-10-year development programs extending beyond 2030.

Affected companies and impact: Vertiv Holdings (VRT: US) — Positive, high magnitude; Eaton (ETN: US) — Positive, high magnitude; Powell Industries (POWL: US) — Positive, high magnitude; nVent Electric (NVT: US) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude; EMCOR Group (EME: US) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude; Comfort Systems USA (FIX: US) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude. Amazon (AMZN: US), Microsoft (MSFT: US), Alphabet (GOOGL: US) and Meta Platforms (META: US) receive a mixed read-through: positive regarding the scale and duration of infrastructure deployment, but negative at a moderate magnitude for near-term free cash flow, construction cost and energization timing.

The principal positive implication is that conventional backlog analysis can understate active data-center infrastructure demand. Rapid purchase orders against master service agreements can convert into revenue during the same quarter, particularly when a contractor already has labor and project-management infrastructure on site. Suppliers serving electrical distribution, switchgear, thermal management, busway, enclosures and MEP systems can therefore experience order acceleration with limited advance visibility in contractors’ reported backlog.

Vertiv, Eaton, Powell and nVent are direct beneficiaries of increasing electrical and thermal content per site. Higher rack density and larger campuses require more power-conversion equipment, distribution systems, switchgear, cooling infrastructure, enclosures and connectivity. EMCOR and Comfort Systems benefit from the broader mechanical and electrical construction requirement, although Quanta’s increasingly integrated offering creates a separate competitive risk addressed later in the report.

The call also indicates that data-center development is increasingly a full-site infrastructure problem rather than a server-procurement problem. Grid interconnection, substations, transmission, generation, civil work, electrical systems, mechanical systems and fabrication all determine when computing equipment can operate. This supports sustained demand across the power and construction chain but increases the probability that infrastructure, rather than semiconductor availability, becomes the limiting factor for AI-capacity deployment.

The near-term catalyst is upside to orders and revenue at power-infrastructure vendors as additional phases are added to active sites. Quanta’s observation that customers request additional services immediately after seeing successful execution indicates potential for intra-project scope expansion. The longer-duration shift is the emergence of multi-year infrastructure campuses in which the same customer repeatedly adds electrical, generation and balance-of-plant scope.

The negative read-through for hyperscalers is that the physical cost of AI capacity continues to rise. Accelerated construction requires premium labor, early equipment procurement, customer advances and potentially temporary behind-the-meter generation. The call therefore confirms the strategic commitment to AI infrastructure but also supports higher capital-expenditure estimates and longer periods before some investments become revenue-producing assets.

No specific hyperscaler was identified on the call. The affected public companies represent the principal large U.S. hyperscale buyers and should be treated as a sector-level read-through rather than disclosed customer relationships.

THE 800-VOLT TRANSITION IS A LONGER-DURATION OPTION, NOT A CURRENT EARNINGS DRIVER (READ-THROUGH 5)

Call evidence: When asked whether Quanta was seeing RFPs for 800-volt data-center architecture, management responded that it had not yet seen the opportunity “show up” commercially. Quanta is involved in engineering and equipment work, but no meaningful RFP activity was identified. Management nevertheless stated that “the higher the voltage, the better for Quanta,” reflecting the company’s preference for technically complex high-voltage infrastructure.

Affected companies and impact: Vertiv Holdings (VRT: US) — Near-term neutral-to-negative, low-to-moderate magnitude; Eaton (ETN: US) — Near-term neutral-to-negative, low magnitude; Schneider Electric (SU: France) — Near-term neutral-to-negative, low magnitude. All 3 receive a positive, moderate-to-high magnitude longer-duration read-through if higher-voltage architectures become standard.

This is an important timing signal. Quanta operates close to actual engineering, site construction and customer procurement decisions. The absence of meaningful RFP activity indicates that the industry remains in design, engineering and early-equipment-development phases rather than broad commercial deployment. Revenue expectations explicitly dependent on large 800-volt deployments during 2026 or early 2027 may therefore be ahead of the physical construction cycle.

The near-term negative is not a demand reversal. It is a mismatch between market narrative and revenue timing. Engineering work can precede major equipment orders by several quarters, particularly when standards, safety requirements, system architectures and supplier qualifications are still evolving. Companies with diversified data-center backlogs should not experience a material earnings impairment solely from this delay, but 800-volt-specific upside may not become visible as quickly as aggressive expectations imply.

The longer-duration read-through remains positive. Higher voltage increases the technical complexity, safety requirements, equipment content and engineering value of the power chain. It can therefore support larger addressable markets and stronger barriers to entry for qualified suppliers and contractors. Quanta’s statement that higher voltage is economically favorable indicates that the architecture could increase value per site rather than merely replace existing low-voltage equipment.

The key near-term catalysts are initial commercial RFPs, customer-standard announcements and supplier disclosures that 800-volt systems have moved from engineering to contracted production. Until those indicators emerge, the call supports treating 800-volt exposure as valuation optionality rather than a material near-term earnings contributor.

DATA-CENTER RESTRICTIONS ARE MORE LIKELY TO REDISTRIBUTE LOAD GEOGRAPHICALLY THAN DESTROY AGGREGATE DEMAND (READ-THROUGH 6)

Call evidence: An analyst raised the possibility of data-center pauses or moratoria in New York and other states. Management indicated that Quanta has little relevant New York exposure, is not seeing a shortage of alternative locations and continues to work on multi-year developments beyond 2030. Management contrasted restrictive markets with rural areas such as northern Louisiana, where large projects can generate employment and tax-base benefits. Quanta also emphasized the importance of securing sufficient power in PJM.

Affected companies and impact: Entergy (ETR: US) — Positive, moderate-to-high magnitude; American Electric Power (AEP: US) — Positive, moderate magnitude; Dominion Energy (D: US) — Mixed, moderate magnitude; Digital Realty Trust (DLR: US) — Positive long-term, moderate magnitude, but mixed near-term.

The core implication is that political resistance is more likely to alter project geography and sequencing than eliminate hyperscale infrastructure demand. Technology companies require power, land, water access, fiber and permitting certainty. When 1 jurisdiction becomes restrictive, projects can migrate toward regions offering faster approvals, available generation, economic-development incentives and utilities willing to construct the required infrastructure.

Entergy is a potential beneficiary because Louisiana and the broader Gulf and Southeast offer land, energy infrastructure and economic-development capacity. American Electric Power has exposure to both PJM load growth and portions of Louisiana through its operating territories, although additional capital requirements and regulatory recovery remain important. Dominion benefits from the strategic value of Virginia’s existing data-center ecosystem, but it also faces the negative side of the read-through: concentrated load growth can intensify transmission, generation, affordability and regulatory challenges.

Digital Realty receives a positive long-term demand signal because aggregate capacity requirements remain durable, but site-level execution becomes more important. A geographically diversified developer can redirect development toward viable markets, while projects dependent on constrained grids or hostile permitting environments may experience lower returns or delayed lease commencement.

The transmission mechanism is a regional divergence in utility load growth, regulated capital spending, land values and generation requirements. Utilities with available power and supportive regulators can secure incremental load and expand rate bases. Utilities in constrained regions may face substantial upfront investment, public opposition and customer-affordability pressure before earnings benefits are realized.

The near-term catalysts are large-load service agreements, new campus announcements, generation commitments and changes in utility capital plans. The longer-duration shift is a redistribution of data-center investment toward markets where the full package of generation, transmission, land and permitting can be delivered with greater certainty.

This is a geographic inference from management’s discussion rather than a disclosure of specific contracts with the listed companies.

text:
In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

text:
For three months, Duke barely moved.

The 14-year-old Labrador spent his days in a shelter with his face turned toward the wall, ignoring visitors, treats, and every family that stopped by his kennel. After his owner, Samuel Bell, passed away, no one in the family realized Duke had been taken to the county shelter. By the time they found him, he had already been overlooked again and again.

Then one morning, everything changed.

Samuel's older brother, Arthur Bell, arrived at the shelter. At 79 years old, he walked slowly with a wooden cane and wore a faded olive-green coat that had once belonged to Samuel.

When a volunteer offered to show him other dogs, Arthur smiled and said, "I'm looking for the oldest one."

Instead of calling Duke's name, Arthur quietly sat outside the kennel.

The moment the sleeve of that old coat brushed against the wire, Duke froze.

He lifted his head, sniffed the familiar scent, struggled to his feet, and slowly walked over. Then he gently buried his face into Arthur's arm, as if he had finally found someone who felt like home.

That's when the volunteer noticed the name on Duke's file. Samuel Bell.

Arthur explained that the coat had been his brother's favorite. Samuel wore it on almost every walk with Duke, and after he passed away, Arthur kept it because it still carried his scent.

That same day, Duke went home.

He quickly claimed the rug beside Arthur's chair as his favorite spot, while Samuel's old coat stayed draped over the armrest until Duke finally stopped checking its pockets.

Months later, Arthur bought a new jacket. But on cold mornings, he still reaches for Samuel's old coat and every single time, Duke is waiting at the door before Arthur's cane even touches the floor.

Some bonds never fade. Sometimes, all it takes is a familiar scent to remind a heart where it belongs. ❤️

text:
This video is an essay tackling the trend in certain religious and online circles of labeling Historically Black Fraternities and Sororities (the Divine Nine or D9) and Prince Hall Masonry as "demonic," "occult," or "satanic."

1. Adult Agency vs. "The Devil Made Me Do It" 

Personal Accountability: The speaker opens by addressing former members who denounce their former organizations. He argues that undergraduates joining fraternities/sororities are adults pursuing status, legacy, and social capital.

Distinction Between Ordeal & Abuse: While strongly condemning abusive, sadistic, or deadly hazing, he defends structured "rites of passage" (testing, discipline, sacrifice) as culturally universal mechanisms for personal growth.

Regret vs. Demonic Accusation: He criticizes former members who enjoyed the status while active, but later—due to personal trauma, disappointment, or religious conversion—reframe their experience as being "hypnotized by the occult" to escape personal accountability.

2. Conspiracy Theories & The "Crossroads" Myth 

Explaining Excellence Through Suspicion: The host links Divine Nine denunciations to a broader pattern in Black public life where discipline and talent are delegitimized by claims of demonic bargains (e.g., the Robert Johnson blues myth or Katt Williams’ "Illuminati" comments on Club Shay Shay).

Lazy Condemnation: Attributing someone's success or an organization's rituals to "demons" is a lazy shortcut that avoids analyzing history, sociology, or human effort.

3. Deconstructing Ancient Symbolism & Rituals 

Symbols🌐Worship: Addressing claims that pagan symbols (such as Minerva in Delta Sigma Theta, the Sphinx in Alpha Phi Alpha, or Damon & Pythias in Omega Psi Phi) imply pagan worship.

The Double Standard: He notes that standard academic education involves studying pagan philosophers (Plato, Aristotle) without being labeled occult.  Furthermore, U.S. government architecture (e.g., the Washington Monument obelisk or Lady Justice at courthouses) uses Greco-Roman/Egyptian motifs without being called a "temple of Satan".

4. Historical Context of Religion, Gnosticism & Church History

Christianity’s Cultural Synthesis: Christianity itself developed by absorbing and adapting surrounding Mediterranean cultures, sacred meals, and mystery traditions.

Gnosticism & Church Councils: Early Christian debates, the designation of "heresy," and ecumenical councils (Nicaea, Chalcedon) demonstrate that Christian orthodoxy was historically forged through human debate, institutional politics, and power struggles—not dropped down pure from heaven.

Imperial & Historical Cruelties: He highlights the hypocrisy of religious zealots condemning D9 symbols while ignoring atrocities committed historically in the name of Christianity (the Crusades, Inquisitions, Salem Witch Trials, and the religious defense of the Transatlantic Slave Trade and colonialism).

5. African Diasporic Survival, Syncretism & Secrecy 

Secrecy as a Survival Tool:  In the African Diaspora (Candomblé, Vodou, Santería, and U.S. Negro Spirituals like "Steal Away to Jesus"), secrecy and coded symbolism were essential mechanisms to preserve culture and organize liberation under brutal oppression.

Cultural Imperialism: Declaring all ritual, secrecy, or non-Christian symbols as "demonic" erases the historical survival strategies of African descendants

6. "Where Are Your Works?" (Legacy & Impact) 

Tangible Fruit: The speaker compares the real-world contributions of Prince Hall Masons and D9 members to the empty noise of online critics.

Historical Figures Produced:

Prince Hall Masons: Richard Allen, A. Philip Randolph, Thurgood Marshall, Medgar Evers, Duke Ellington.

Divine Nine: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., W.E.B. Du Bois, Coretta Scott King, Shirley Chisholm, John Lewis, Mae Jemison, Charles Drew, Michael Jordan, and Langston Hughes.

Call to Action: He challenges religious zealots to show their own schools, civil rights accomplishments, mentoring programs, or institutions before casting judgments over legacy builders.

💡 Commentary / Opinion

Nail on the Head regarding "Sour Grace":  The video offers a sharp sociological critique of how modern internet culture handles institutional regret, Reframing personal disappointment as a "spiritual warfare" narrative is often a way to gain viral clout or absolve oneself of personal choices.

Nuanced View on Hazing:  He successfully maintains a balanced position—refusing to excuse real abuse/hazing while defending the legitimate utility of structured, non-abusive rites of passage.

Effective Historical Counter-Arguments:  Using American civic architecture and early church history he effectively highlights the logical inconsistency of the "symbolism = demonism" argument.

Tone & Delivery:  Grounded in a pragmatic, no-nonsense style ("straight up, no chaser"), it speaks directly to Black cultural discourse, bridging academic historical analysis with street-smart rationalism.

text:
Dolly Parton stood just 5 feet   nothing, yet her music towered over America’s country scene for six decades.
​As word of the death of the iconic   singer, actress, philanthropist, and   businesswoman circulated on Aug. 25, tributes poured in from across the   country and beyond as flags were flown at half-staff.
The 80-year-old star’s passing caused many, from the humble to the powerful, to pause in   recognition of her unique place in American culture.
“Very sad to report that Dolly   Parton, one of the greatest Country   singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away. This is a true loss for   millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will.   Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you,” President Donald Trump wrote   on Truth Social.
​Her musical legacy includes 113   songs on Billboard’s Hot Country   Songs chart. Of those, 25 reached No. 1—the most by any female artist.
​During her rise to fame in the   1960s, she became one of the most   prolific female singer-songwriters of her generation. Yet Parton never forgot   her east Tennessee values.
Born in 1946 in a one-room cabin in an Appalachian holler, she was one of 12   children. After learning to play the guitar as a girl, she began performing   at her church and appeared on local radio and television shows.
​Parton joined forces with Porter   Wagoner, known for his pompadour and   rhinestone-studded Western suits. They made their official debut performance   as a duo at The Grand Ole Opry on Nov. 25, 1967.
That moment marked a   milestone for Parton, who had finally   made it to Nashville, the country music capital of the world. There, she was   destined to overshadow her mentor, demonstrating a rare talent that   transcended country music.
‘Face of Country Music’
​Gary Scott Thomas, a longtime country radio show host and podcaster, said he   remembers seeing Parton and Wagoner playing in the back of a flatbed trailer   out in a field in Red Level, Alabama. The year was 1970, and it was his first   country concert.
​“Her hair was as big as she was,” he told The Epoch Times. “She was known for her curvy figure.   But what drew you in was her smile. There was nothing about that woman that   just did not radiate joy.”
Sierra Bernal, a Nashville   songwriter and recording artist, said   that Parton stayed true to her hillbilly roots.
One of her favorite Parton quotes was “It takes a lot of money to look this cheap.” It was pure   Dolly, a testament to how she navigated fame and fortune with grace and   laughter.
Her hit song “Jolene” arguably solidified Parton’s place as a country music legend. The 1972   ballad resonated with women everywhere, with its blunt woman-to-woman lyrics   pushing it to No. 1 on the country charts.
​In the song, based on a real-life encounter with a pretty bank teller who   flirted with her husband, Parton pleaded with a copper-haired vixen not to   steal her man.
​“I had to have this talk with you/ My happiness depends on you/ And whatever you decide to do, Jolene,”   she sang.
Yet the song that stood apart for its aching lyrics was “I Will Always Love You.” The 1974   release came as Parton was parting ways with her longtime partner, Wagoner.
​That song went on to become the smash cover by the late Whitney Houston for   the Hollywood movie “The Bodyguard,” in which she starred opposite Kevin   Costner.
Big Hair, Bigger Business
​Outside of music, she branched out into different business and philanthropic   ventures.
In 1986, she opened a theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, near her birthplace and named it   after herself. Dollywood attracts more than 3 million guests annually, even   as others struggle to keep their doors open today.
In 1995, Parton started the   Imagination Library to boost   education in one Tennessee county in honor of her own father, who never   learned to read or write.
It now sends books nationwide and   beyond, and the library has given   more than 300 million books to children younger than 5.
Parton herself never had children during her 59-year marriage to Carl Thomas Dean, who   died in March 2025, but she was surrounded by a multitude of nieces and   nephews, whom she lavished with new cars and college educations.​

Parton said in more than one   interview that she felt that it was   part of God’s plan for her, “so everybody’s kids” could be hers.
—Darlene McCormick Sanchez
BOOKMARKS
OpenAI revealed this week that 700   of its AI agents—AI programs that run with minimal human intervention—were the ones   that hacked into another AI company’s system. “This incident is the first   known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without   authorization,” OpenAI said in an investigative report it published on Aug. 26.

Hundreds are dead, and many more   are still missing after a flood in Nepal this week. Arthur Zhang has eyewitness accounts of the   disaster in his latest report.
Russia warned on Aug. 27 that it   could strike British and French military targets both inside and outside   Ukraine, following the UK’s pledge to share classified technical intelligence   to help Kyiv build its own long-range cruise missiles. “They should   understand this is ‘playing with fire’ and that the consequences could be   unpredictable, including for them,” the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs   said in a post on X.
Hungary formally condemned Russia’s military aggression this week in a move that marks a   sharp shift in Budapest’s outlook under its new government. “Russia’s conduct   constitutes a threat to Hungary, to Europe and to the global order,” a set of   policy guidelines signed by Prime Minister Peter Magyar said.
General Mills said all of its   cereals sold in the United States are now made without certified artificial colors, completing a goal the food giant set for this summer. “This   achievement reflects how we are evolving with consumer needs while continuing   to offer food that tastes great, delivers quality and provides value,”   Bethany Quam, president of Big G Cereal at General Mills, said in a   statement.
—Stacy Robinson

As much as I like you guys, I’m going to be busy today with work, church, and family stuff.

But I need to share a crazy story from last night. I think I saved the lives of two girls.

I was coming from Huntsville late at night. It’s a long drive back home. I managed to get a trip from Huntsville to The Woodlands, and another from The Woodlands to Houston. At the end of that last trip, I was close enough that I could drive home without feeling like I was wasting miles, but far enough away that I might still get a good trip to take me closer to home.

I saw several trips come up on the app. I didn’t like any of them. I was about to turn the app off when I saw the perfect trip. I’d pick someone up close to where I was and drop them off close to where I live. Good pay, too. I almost didn’t take it because I was tired and it was already past 1 a.m., but how was I going to say no to basically free money?

I get to the street and quickly realize this isn’t a street. It’s a back alley. Houses on both sides, but it’s a back alley. The map says the pickup location is at the end of the alley, where it meets the next street. But it shows their location more toward the middle. I never know whether to trust the app, and I see people at the end of the alley. I wait where the app marks their current location, and no one comes out. I called three times, but the calls failed each time. Then they message me: meet us at the street.

So I assume they mean the corner, where the pickup location is marked on the app. I send a message asking if that’s what they mean, but I start heading that way slowly. Suddenly I get another message:

Drive back to where you were.

This is an alley. I can’t do a U-turn. I have to drive in reverse. It’s dark. I could have just canceled the trip and gone home. It felt creepy. Suddenly the girls pop up out of nowhere. They get in and immediately get hysterical. They’re telling me they got beaten up by a bunch of people. Badly beaten up. No broken bones, but they had bruises all over, heads full of bumps, swollen, blood, everything hurting.

“We got beat up by a bunch of people. They want to kill us. We were hiding in the bushes. Go! Go!”

It was crazy. I dropped them off in a rich neighborhood. These were two rich girls who went to a party in a ghetto neighborhood and got beaten up by a bunch of people over a stupid argument. One of the girls was hysterical the entire way. The other was holding up much better and trying to comfort her friend. I offered to take them to the hospital, but they refused. I told them to call 911, but I don’t think they wanted to do that. I think they said they would call from home.

Had I not been in that area at that time and taken the trip, who knows how long they would have had to hide behind the bushes in that dark alley. Also, it was stupid of me to go into that dark alley, but I’m glad I did. Poor girls. I was shaking when I got home, thinking about how close I came to not picking them up.
